Introduction The advent of distributed word representations has revolutionized the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP), enabling computers to capture complex semantic information inherent in language and leverage it for a wide range of downstream tasks, including but not limited to sentiment analysis, question classification, and language modeling. Originating from the seminal work of word2vec (Mikolov et al., 2013), which introduces continuous bag-of-words and skip-gram models to generate vector representations of words, this paradigm soon gains widespread adoption and evolves into Word Embeddings (WE). The dominance of WE in NLP stems from its ability to distill the co-occurrence information within a large corpus into numeric representations that can be fed into neural networks or used as stand-alone features, overcoming the curse of dimensionality and the one-hot problem associated with categorical variables. However, conventional WE rely heavily on the inherent structure of the target language, and as such often perform poorly on languages with unique characteristics, such as Chinese. Unlike English, which has an alphabetic writing system, Chinese is composed entirely of logograms, each of which represents a word or a concept. Consequently, individual Chinese characters carry highly linguistic significance, serving as both the building blocks of words and potential indicators of their meaning. A major design challenge for WE is that these linguistic properties are not inherently reflected in the dense numerical representations. As a result, many state-of-the-art WE methods specifically tailored for Chinese languages, such as WordPiece (Wu et al., 2016) and BERT (Devlin et al., 2019), often incorporate special techniques like character splitting, subwording, or pre-training with character-level language models to expose the underlying character structure. In contrast, we propose a novel and more direct approach to developing effective WE for Chinese, one that not only utilizes but also preserves the inherent properties of Chinese characters. This consists of two component-enhanced Chinese character embedding models, and their extensions to include bigram information. The critical innovation of our approach lies in the intentional division of each Chinese word into its constituent parts (subwords) during training and inference, effectively allowing the model to take advantage of the grammatical and semantic contributions of individual characters. We then evaluate the effectiveness of these methods through a battery of experiments designed to assess their ability to accurately predict semantic relations between word pairs and classify nuanced semantic categories in text, showing encouraging results and suggesting a brighter future for NLP tasks on Chinese language.

Discriminative Strategies to Integrate Multiword Expression Recognition and Parsing The recognition and incorporation of multiword expressions (MWEs) into natural language processing (NLP) systems has been a topic of significant interest over the past few years. MWEs, which are phrases or groups of words that function as a single unit with a meaning that cannot be derived from the sum of the individual words, hold crucial information that can greatly enhance the accuracy of various NLP tasks. A key challenge in leveraging the power of MWEs is their identification and integration into parsing models, which are essential components of many NLP applications. Various studies have demonstrated the benefits of integrating MWEs into parsing procedures in controlled settings, where all MWEs have been accurately identified beforehand. However, the true value of these approaches remains unclear when they are applied in real-world settings, where the preidentification of MWEs is often not straightforward. In such contexts, the integration of MWEs is typically hampered by the inherent difficulties associated with MWE recognition accuracy and the coupling between MWE recognition and parsing errors. This paper seeks to fill the knowledge gap by investigating two highly discriminative strategies for the integration of MWEs in a real constituency parsing setting. Unlike previous studies, which predominantly focused on the intrinsic benefits of integrating MWEs, our approach ardently acknowledges that in reality, the impact is likely to be tempered by two factors: variability in MWE recognition and coupled estimation issues. Our first strategy relies on the preexecution of a state-of-the-art MWE recognizer to preidentify MWEs before parsing, while the second approach embeds the recognition of MWEs into the parser's grammar followed by a reranker uniquely suited for correcting the parsing initialization and handling egregious MWE errors. Both proposed strategies represent an effort to harness the power of MWEs in low-ideal regimes where available data is limited and precision of MWE recognition falls off dramatically. Introduction Grammatical error correction (GEC) is a vital task in natural language processing (NLP) that endeavors to automatically detect and correct grammatical, spelling, and inflectional errors in text. With the increasing demand for high-quality language processing systems, developing effective GEC models has become a pressing issue in the NLP community. Recent years have witnessed significant advancements in GEC through the application of neural machine translation (NMT) technology, which has brought about substantial improvements in error detection and correction rates. However, despite these advancements, existing GEC models still incur limitations due to their inability to effectively capture and correct local errors in spelling and inflection. These errors, although seemingly minor, can impede the overall coherence and readability of the text, negatively affecting its conveyance of intended meaning. Moreover, prior NMT-based GEC models often rely on a monolithic attention mechanism that, while effective in handling global errors in word order and usage, is less adept at identifying and correcting localized errors, which typically involve more minor alterations in orthography (i.e., spelling, capitalization, and punctuation). Such limitations stem from the intrinsic constraints of current GEC frameworks, which sometimes fail to effectively capture and incorporate crucial contextual information spanning both word and character levels. Hence, to meaningfully improve the proficiency and representativeness of GEC systems, there is a pressing need for the development of innovative, efficient, and hybrid models that can effectively rival and outperform their predecessors on benchmarks such as the CoNLL-14 dataset. This paper addresses the aforementioned challenges and limitations by introducing a novel, hybrid neural model specifically designed for the task of GEC. By incorporating two nested attention layers, the proposed model leverages the capabilities of both word-level and character-level attention mechanisms to more effectively capture and incorporate crucial contextual information in the form of both global word order and usage patterns, as well as localized spelling and inflectional features. Through experimentation and benchmark evaluation on the widely used CoNLL-14 dataset, we demonstrate that the proposed hybrid model significantly outperforms previous state-of-the-art NMT-based GEC models, achieving superior error detection and correction rates. Further analysis reveals that the superiority of the proposed model can be largely attributed to the pervasive and effective application of the nested attention mechanism, particularly in the course of correcting localized errors in orthography. These findings contribute substantially to our current understanding of the relationships between the distribution of contextual information, attention mechanisms, and GEC model performance, and have critical implications for the future development of more advanced and accurate GEC systems.

Pluralizing Nouns across Agglutinating Bantu Languages The task of pluralizing nouns is a crucial component in various text generation applications, including context-sensitive user interfaces, chatbots, and natural language generation systems. While significant advances have been made in automating this process for widely spoken languages, such as English and Spanish, less attention has been devoted to languages belonging to the Bantu family. Bantu languages, comprising over 500 distinct varieties, present a unique set of challenges due to their intricate morphological and syntactic structures. Specifically, agglutinating Bantu languages are characterized by their use of a series of prefixes attached to roots to convey grammatical information, such as number, case, and gender. Despite belonging to different language zones, recent studies have shown similarities in the approach to pluralizing nouns for languages like isiZulu and Runyankore, suggesting that bootstrapping and generalizability might be feasible. This observation highlights the need for a more comprehensive understanding of the complex morphological and syntactic mechanisms underlying Bantu languages. The development of a generic pluralizer for Bantu languages, one that can be applied across multiple languages, would have significant implications for language technology, enabling more effective natural language processing and generation for this diverse group of languages. A major obstacle to the creation of such a pluralizer is the existing inadequate specification of noun classes in Meinhof's 1948 work. Meinhof identified only 29 noun classes, which have been widely accepted and utilized in Bantu linguistics. However, for computational purposes, these classes are insufficient due to the non-determinism of prefixes in many Bantu languages. To address this limitation, we redefined the characteristic noun class tables to include 53 classes, providing a more nuanced understanding of the morphological structure of these languages. Our research aims to provide a systematic investigation of the pluralization of nouns across seven Bantu languages, representing three different Guthrie language zones. By exploring the morphological and syntactic patterns underlying these languages, we aimed to create a generic pluralizer capable of accurately pluralizing nouns for these languages. The results presented in this paper demonstrate the feasibility of this approach, highlighting the potential for a generic pluralizer that achieves comparable accuracy to language-specific models for isiZulu and Runyankore. Our findings not only contribute to the development of more effective language technology but also provide a critical step towards a more inclusive language processing framework that supports the diverse linguistic profiles of Bantu languages. In the following sections, we present our methodological approach, the results of our experiments, and a critical discussion of our findings.

Joint Generation of Transliterations from Multiple Representations Transliteration, often referred to as phonetic translation, plays a pivotal role in various natural language processing (NLP) applications such as machine translation, text-to-speech synthesis, and information retrieval. By transliterating words from their original script to a target script, it enables the representation of words in a different but phonetically equivalent form. This facilitates the processing and analysis of texts in languages with non-latinate scripts. A key challenge in machine transliteration is effectively capturing the complexities of both pronunciation and spelling, which are often intertwined and nuanced. Conventional transliteration approaches typically rely on either spelling or pronunciation information alone to generate transliterations. For instance, spelling-based methods focus on the morphological and orthographical characteristics of words in the source script, whereas pronunciation-based approaches emphasize the phonetic and acoustic properties of words. While these methods have achieved notable success, they are prone to limitations such as inconsistent transliteration quality, inadequate handling of exceptions, and lack of adaptability to diverse scripts. Furthermore, existing methods often neglect the valuable information that is embedded in both spelling and pronunciation features, leading to suboptimal transliteration results. Recent advancements in deep learning and NLP have led to the emergence of joint learning methods that aim to leverage multi-source information for improved representational capabilities. The integration of multiple representations, including both spelling and pronunciation features, is particularly promising for addressing the transliteration challenge. By jointly modeling the interplay between spelling and pronunciation, these methods can more effectively capture the intricacies of language and improve transliteration quality. Motivated by the potential benefits of joint learning, this paper presents an effective framework for joint generation of transliterations from multiple representations. Our proposed method not only effectively incorporates information from both spelling and pronunciation but also extends this capability to include transliterations from other languages. To further enhance the accuracy and robustness of our framework, we incorporate reranking and lexicon features that allow for an even more nuanced and contextualized understanding of language. Through an extensive evaluation on several benchmark datasets, we demonstrate the superiority of our joint learning approach over traditional and state-of-the-art methods, showcasing significant improvements in transliteration accuracy. By providing a comprehensive treatment of joint transliteration generation, our paper makes several key contributions to the field of NLP. Firstly, our proposed framework offers a novel and effective solution to the longstanding challenge of capturing the complexities of transliteration.

Introduction The rapid growth of online social platforms has led to a tremendous rise in microblogging, instant messaging, and short-form text-based communication. However, the informal and colloquial nature of these text styles poses significant challenges for Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks. One of the primary issues is the limited availability of annotated corpora specifically designed for microblog texts, which are often lexically, grammatically, and stylistically different from standard texts. As a result, many existing NLP methods that rely on standard annotated resources may exhibit poor performance on microblog texts. Word segmentation, part-of-speech (POS) tagging, and text normalization are three fundamental tasks in NLP, each of which plays a crucial role in various downstream applications such as information retrieval, sentiment analysis, and machine translation. Traditional approaches to these tasks often treat them as independent problems, focusing on one task at a time. However, joint modeling of these tasks has been shown to be effective in leveraging the dependencies between them, leading to improved performance and efficiency. In this paper, we propose a transition-based model for joint word segmentation, POS-tagging, and text normalization. The core idea is to design a unified framework that addresses these tasks simultaneously, leveraging the strengths of each task to complement the others. Our approach is inherently different from existing methods in that it can be trained on standard text corpora, potentially overcoming the lack of annotated microblog corpora that plagues previous methods. This is achieved through the use of a sophisticated transition-based model, which allows the model to learn the dependencies between tasks and adapt to the complexities of microblog texts. To evaluate our model, we develop a large-scale annotated corpus based on microblog texts, which will serve as a benchmark for future research in this area. Experimental results show that our joint model can significantly improve the performance of word segmentation on microblog texts, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach in handling the unique challenges of informal and colloquial language. The error reduction in segmentation accuracy achieved by our model is substantial, with an impressive 12.02% reduction compared to the traditional approach. This work has far-reaching implications for a wide range of NLP applications, particularly those that involve short-form text-based communication. By providing a more accurate and efficient way to handle word segmentation, POS-tagging, and text normalization in microblog texts, our model can facilitate more effective information extraction, sentiment analysis, and language understanding in various domains.

Advancing Linguistic Features and Insights by Label-informed Feature Grouping: An Exploration in the Context of Native Language Identification The field of Linguistic and Natural Language Processing (NLP) has witnessed significant advancements in recent years, largely due to the availability of large-scale datasets and the development of sophisticated machine learning algorithms. However, despite these breakthroughs, native language identification (NLI) remains a daunting task that continues to pose significant challenges for both researchers and practitioners alike. One of the primary hurdles to successful NLI is the inherent sparsity of linguistic features, which hinders the model's ability to capture the complexities of language data. This sparsity arises from the fact that linguistic features often exhibit relational and context-dependent properties, making it challenging to define and capture their relationships in a scalable and generalizable manner. Traditional approaches to NLI rely heavily on hand-crafted feature engineering, which is typically performed in a data- and model-agnostic manner. This feature engineering paradigm, while effective in its early stages, begins to falter as the dimensionality of the feature space increases and the data availability becomes limited. Furthermore, the lack of interpretability and the subjective nature of feature engineering limit the potential for generalizability and replicability of results. In this paper, we propose a novel hierarchical clustering approach that endeavours to address these limitations by grouping linguistic features based on their correlations with the target class label. This label-informed feature grouping (LFG) approach, inspired by the principles of variationist linguistics, offers a promising solution for mitigating data sparsity and enhancing the model's ability to capture the nuances of linguistic data. The variationist approach views language as a dynamic and constantly evolving system, where the choice of linguistic structures is affected by a multitude of social and historical factors. Within this framework, linguistic features are not seen as isolated entities but rather as part of a complex network of relationships, each influencing the others in subtle but significant ways. Our proposed LFG approach leverages this insight by facilitating the clustering of linguistic features into cohesive groups, where each group behaves similarly with respect to the target class. This grouping process abstracts away from the individual feature occurrences, allowing the model to focus on the relationships between groups rather than individual features. By doing so, we aim to enable the model to better capture the subtleties of linguistic data and improve the overall performance of NLI tasks.

However, the underlying causes or effects of these events often remain unexplained, limiting the scope of their usefulness. This challenge arises from the fact that causal relationships between time series events generally incur high complexity and heterogeneity, exhibited through various data types - continuous, categorical, and text. To effectively address the challenges of extracting causality between time series and their corresponding textual explanations, it is crucial to leverage not only the patterns inherent in time series data but also the contextual information contained within the text data companion to the series. Nonetheless, constructing an effective bridge that connects these two disparate data sources is a highly complex task. For instance, directly perusing text data might result in missing implicit patterns and relationships exhibited by the time series, whereas, mainstream time series analysis often falls short in capturing the highly linguistic causal relevant features. This challenge is compounded by various limitations of traditional time series analysis, which find it difficult to capture certain context-variables present within the narratives of time series. First, the identification of causal entities from text, and second, the construction of a meaningful explanation spanning across the identified causal entities by linking the time series data to the explanatory text. Introduction Determining whether a given claim is supported by evidence lies at the heart of natural language processing (NLP). This fundamental problem is perhaps most elegantly captured by the paradigm of Textual Entailment (TE), a subfield of NLP that seeks to assess the validity of statements or claims in the context of available evidence. Textual Entailment has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its crucial role in Information Extraction, Sentiment Analysis, and a range of other NLP applications. Despite its importance, dealing with vast collections of text that may support or refute a given claim poses substantial challenges, compounded by the fact that the evidence needed to support a claim might differ significantly from that required to refute it. Most existing research solutions grapple with this challenge by isolating two critical tasks: recognizing evidence that may pertain to a claim and evaluating the claim by integrating the identified evidence. This sequential, pipeline-based approach can often lead to reduced quality and limited ability to flexibly adapt to varying evidence set sizes. Moreover, decoupling these two important aspects not only hampers the holistic evaluation of a claim but also necessitates the development and training of separate models, thereby sometimes compromising the accuracy of individual tasks due to a potential lack of shared knowledge during training. In this paper, we seek to revise this standard approach through our proposed system, TWOWINGOS, designed as a novel Two-Wing Optimization Strategy for Evidential Claim Verification. As our name suggests, TWOWINGOS strives to mark a crucial shift towards end-to-end verification by integrating both evidence identification and claim validation, such that these complementary tasks are run in tandem throughout the optimization process. We assert that coupling these two aspects not only enables our system to integrate a diverse set of evidence and be adaptable in its operation without going through series of transformations, but it also preserves shared information through a jointly trained model, thereby allowing each individual task to benefit and fortify one another. Our major contributions lie in formulating the Evidential Claim Verification task as a coupled optimization problem for the first time, implying that our system operates independently on these two coequal but interdependent components. By merging claim verification and evidence identification within a single model training loop, we automate the optimization of both aspects of our system. Furthermore, our novel architectural view of combining the related tasks yields the facility to reuse the retrieved evidence for claim verification without additional retraining.

Measuring Lexical Cohesion: Beyond Word Repetition The accurate identification of topical shifts in discourse is a fundamental challenge in natural language processing (NLP). Topical shifts are pivotal in comprehending text coherence and, subsequently, impact the overall efficiency of various NLP applications, such as text summarization, information retrieval, and question answering. Traditionally, topical segmentation is achieved through the lexically-based approaches, which focus on identifying changes in vocabulary to signal a potential topical shift. This method relies on the assumption that certain words, or more specifically, certain types of words, are more likely to appear in one topic rather than another. The logic behind this assumption is simple – as the topic changes, so does the vocabulary. However, this approach has several limitations and room for improvement. Firstly, recognizing topical shifts solely based on word repetition is not always effective, particularly when dealing with certain genres, such as technical and scientific texts, or even literary narratives that employ deliberately ambiguous language. For example, a topic may not be explicitly mentioned in a text but still be implicit in the context, which is more relevant to, say, law and medicine than other domains. Consequently, word repetition sometimes fails to capture the true essence of topical shifts, resulting in incorrect segmentation. A major aim of contemporary NLP is to develop methods that can elucidate these flaws and reach beyond word-based approaches, potentially improving topical segmentation performance. Beyond this challenge of genre dependence, the vocabulary-related approach also fails to account for the variability of human expression. Human languages are characterized by a multitude of linguistic features beyond simple vocabulary changes. For instance, even if the vocabulary employed in a text remains consistent, but describing a concept with varying levels of detail (a broad term versus specific details), the information conveyed and how it is presented are inherently distinct. It is not simply a matter of counting discrete word tokens but rather of examining the relationships between words, meaning, and referencing. Another crucial aspect that has been largely overlooked in previous approaches is the facilitating role of referring expressions in creating topical cohesion. A referring expression is any word that directly refers to an antecedent, which could be a noun phrase, a pronoun, an adjective, etc. A fundamental distinction often overlooked in the literature is how referring expressions participate in conveying topical transitions. Recent research indicates that a referring expression's "density" – the quantity and quality of information that the expression conveys – directly correlates with the degree of accessibility of its antecedent.

Training Dependency Parsers by Jointly Optimizing Multiple Objectives The rise of natural language processing (NLP) has brought about an increasing recognition of the importance of dependency parsing, a task that is central to understanding the structure of human language. A dependency parser is an algorithm that identifies the grammatical relationships between words in a sentence, allowing it to function as a crucial component in various NLP applications, such as machine translation, sentiment analysis, and question answering. Despite the significant progress made in this field, the design of effective training objectives remains an open challenge. The standard supervised parsing objective function, typically used to train dependency parsers, relies on the accuracy of the parser in capturing the correct grammatical structure of a sentence. However, optimizing a parser solely based on this primary objective may lead to suboptimal performance on other important tasks, such as machine translation or parsing unseen domains, due to the lack of information regarding the intrinsic parsing quality or the extrinsic quality of the parser's output. As a response to this limitation, researchers have started exploring alternative approaches that focus on incorporating additional objectives, such as extrinsic loss functions, to improve the robustness and performance of dependency parsers on multiple downstream tasks. These extrinsic objectives capture the idea of measuring the quality of the parser's output based on its performance on specific tasks, such as machine translation or syntax-based sentence encoding. While these approaches have shown promise, they are often limited by their inability to be effectively combined and optimized with the standard supervised parsing objective. This is largely due to the need for careful hyperparameter tuning and the difficulty in selecting the appropriate weights for the different objectives. Therefore, in this paper, we propose a novel online learning algorithm that addresses these challenges by allowing for the joint optimization of multiple objectives in the training of dependency parsers. Our approach extends the standard supervised parsing objective with additional loss functions, either based on intrinsic parsing quality or the extrinsic quality of the parser's output on specific tasks. Furthermore, we demonstrate the effectiveness of this algorithm on two different dependency parsing architectures: the traditional graph-based parser and the more recent transition-based parser. The results of our experiments provide conclusive evidence of the benefits of jointly optimizing multiple objectives, as they reveal significant improvements in the performance of both parser types on multiple target tasks.

Introduction The ability to automatically analyze semantic similarity in comparable text has become increasingly important in natural language processing, with applications in information retrieval, text summarization, and question answering. Comparable text refers to two or more text segments that convey similar information but may differ in wording, syntax, and semantics. Measuring semantic similarity in this context is crucial for tasks such as finding relevant texts, identifying parallel sentences, and improving the accuracy of text classification. Existing approaches to assessing semantic similarity in comparable text rely heavily on statistical methods that focus on lexical, syntactic, and semantic features [1, 2]. While these methods have shown promising results, they often fail to capture the rich structural information encoded in the syntactic trees of natural language sentences. Syntactic trees represent the hierarchical relationships between words in a sentence and can provide valuable insights into the semantic meaning of the text [3]. Furthermore, the alignment of syntactic trees from comparable text can serve as a strong indicator of semantic similarity, as aligned trees tend to exhibit similar structural patterns and semantic relationships [4]. To overcome the limitations of existing methods, we propose a novel approach that combines syntactic tree matching with a memory-based graph matcher (MBGM). Our method, which we refer to as autoSEM (automatic SEMantic similarity analysis), leverages the power of syntactic tree matching to align comparable text sentences and labels the alignments according to one of five semantic similarity relations. By integrating exhaustive pairwise classification with a combinatorial optimization algorithm, autoSEM is able to perform both tasks simultaneously, providing a comprehensive and accurate measure of semantic similarity. The motivation behind autoSEM stems from the observation that many real-world applications require a detailed understanding of semantic similarity in comparable text. For instance, in the context of parallel text mining, identifying equivalent sentences and phrases is essential for building high-quality machine translation models [5]. Similarly, in text classification tasks, understanding the semantic similarity between comparative text can significantly improve the accuracy of classification models [6]. This paper presents the autoSEM algorithm and evaluates its performance on a monolingual treebank consisting of comparable Dutch news texts. Our experimental results demonstrate that autoSEM performs substantially above the baseline and close to the human reference, providing strong evidence for its effectiveness in capturing semantic similarity in comparable text. By advancing the state of the art in this area, we hope to inspire further research into the automatic analysis of semantic similarity and its applications in natural language processing and related fields.

Using a Dependency Parser to Improve SMT for Subject-Object-Verb Languages Subject-Object-Verb (SOV) languages, such as Japanese and Korean, present unique challenges to statistical machine translation (SMT) systems due to their distinctive word order and syntactic structures. Despite the significant advances in SMT over the past few years, phrase-based systems often struggle to accurately capture the nuances of SOV languages, resulting in suboptimal translations and decreased translation quality. One of the primary hurdles to improving SMT for SOV languages is the difficulty of effectively incorporating linguistic knowledge into the translation process. Traditionally, SMT systems rely on heuristic reordering methods, which often fail to capture the complexities of natural language. Recent advances have led to the development of more sophisticated reordering approaches, such as the use of phrase-based reordering models and word-level reordering techniques. However, these methods often come at the cost of increased computational complexity and require significant amounts of data for training. Furthermore, the incorporation of linguistic knowledge into SMT systems remains an open problem, with most approaches relying on manually-crafted rules and heuristics that are often language-specific and brittle. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to improving SMT for SOV languages based on the use of a dependency parser. Dependency parsing has become a crucial component in many NLP applications, as it provides a robust and efficient way to analyze sentence syntax and structure. By leveraging a dependency parser, our approach can efficiently incorporate linguistic knowledge into SMT systems without increasing the complexity of decoding. This is achieved by reordering the input sentence based on the parsed dependency tree, allowing the SMT system to better capture the nuances of SOV languages. Our hypothesis is that by using a dependency parser to reorder the input sentence, we can significantly improve the accuracy of SMT systems for SOV languages. We evaluate our approach on a set of five SOV languages (Japanese, Korean, Vietnamese, Thai, and Indonesian) and compare its performance to other reordering approaches in state-of-the-art phrase-based SMT systems. Our results demonstrate that our approach leads to substantial improvements in BLEU scores when translating from English, indicating the promise of leveraging dependency parsers for improving SMT for SOV languages. In the following sections, we describe our approach in detail, present our experimental setup and results, and discuss the implications of our findings for future research in SMT and NLP.

TimeML Events Recognition and Classification: Learning CRF Models with Semantic Roles Introduction Recognizing and classifying temporal events within natural language text is a critical task in various natural language processing applications, including question-answering systems, sentiment analysis, and conversational dialogue systems. Temporal information extraction (IE) aims at automatically identifying temporal events, their participants, and their temporal relationships, making it a key component in understanding the structure and meaning of texts. The TimeML (Time Markup Language) standard provides a widely accepted framework for representing temporal events and their associated temporal information. Recent advancements in deep learning and the availability of large annotated corpora have led to the development of robust models for event recognition and classification. However, previous research has shown that morphosyntactic features, such as part-of-speech (POS) tags, named entity recognition (NER), and dependency parsing, can significantly contribute to the performance of event recognition systems. However, these approaches often struggle in dealing with the nuances of human language, including ambiguity, context dependency, and hypothetical situations. One promising approach to address these challenges is to incorporate semantic roles, which represent the roles that entities play in an event, into the event recognition and classification pipeline. Semantic roles have been extensively used in various NLP tasks, including argument role labeling and question-answering systems. They provide a powerful means of capturing the semantic relationships between entities and events, enabling more accurate event recognition and classification. Building upon this idea, this paper proposes a novel approach to TimeML event recognition and classification based on conditional random fields (CRFs), a probabilistic discriminative model for labeling sequential data. We explore the use of a variety of morphosyntactic features, including POS tags, NER, and dependency parsing, in combination with semantic roles features to improve the accuracy of event recognition and classification. Our approach is motivated by the hypothesis that incorporating semantic roles into the model can provide additional insights into the event structure, leading to more accurate classification and recognition results. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on a TimeML annotated corpus and discuss the contribution of semantic roles to the performance of the presented system. Our results show that the application of semantic roles significantly improves the performance of the event recognition system, particularly for nominal events. In what follows, we provide an overview of the related work and background knowledge required to understand our approach, which includes a discussion of the TimeML standard, CRFs, and semantic roles.

Introduction Probabilistic parsing and evaluation of content are fundamental challenges in various natural language processing (NLP) and machine learning tasks, such as machine translation, question answering, and text summarization. The development of effective methods for computing the probability of prefix strings in probabilistic grammars has long been an active area of research in computational linguistics. Among the various frameworks proposed in the literature, Synchronous Context-Free Grammars (SCFGs) [1] have gained significant attention due to their ability to model complex syntactic and semantic dependencies in a scalable manner. In particular, SCFGs have been widely adopted in statistical machine translation (SMT), where they are employed to model the alignment between source and target language sentences. The probability of a score sequence, which is inherently Markovian and synchronous, is an essential component of this framework. The probability of a prefix, on the other hand, is a fundamental and related concept often overlooked in the context of Synchronous Context-Free Grammars. It is, however, of crucial importance in various machine learning and NLP applications, where the ability to predict the likelihood of partially observed input is often a key performance metric. Current approaches to prefix probability computation often heavily rely upon specialized algorithms and theoretically refined normalization techniques [2], which can be computationally and theoretically limiting, mainly because these solutions focus on specific cases or overlook their general application. Other methods apply probabilistic logic for normalization [3] that only subtly increase efficiency with necessity for SCFGs. Their ability to cope with these normal forms and although successful have found their applications relatively few compared to other, such as in SRP/NM Probability [4]. Therefore, there is a pressing need for a general framework that can handle the computation of prefix probabilities for SCFGs, with a wide applicability across various NLP and machine learning tasks. This paper seeks to address this limitation by presenting a novel, wide-ranging framework for computing prefix probabilities for SCFGs. Building upon a simple and novel grammar transformation, combined with established techniques for bringing grammars into normal forms, our framework allows efficient and accurate computation of prefix probabilities for a wide range of SCFGs. The simplicity of its underlying principles, free from specialized algorithms, assures the framework's viability and sensitivity to future improvements. This paper begins by outlining a simple yet effective method for transforming SCFGs into several more tractable forms. We then evaluate the effect of the proposed transformations in evaluating the principal use case precondition based on diverse sourced statistical evaluation.

Structured Perceptron with Inexact Search Most structured prediction models are based on supervised learning methods, notably the structured perceptron (Collins, 2002). These models rely heavily on the assumption that inference can be computed exactly, which favors efficient algorithms such as Viterbi search (Viterbi, 1967). However, in many cases, structured prediction involves complex inference computations that are intractable or have high computational costs. To circumvent this issue, approximate inference methods are widely used in practice, with beam search being a popular choice (Taskar et al., 2004). Unfortunately, the theoretical underpinnings of many of these approximations have yet to be fully explored, leaving researchers to rely on heuristic methods whose performance and convergence properties are often unexplored. Traditional structured perceptrons operate by computing the standard perceptron update rule based on the predicted and true labels, using the full set of inferences that maximize the structured perceptron objective (Collins, 2002). This approach relies on having a hypothetical "oracle" inferences that compute the maximum of the structured loss, which can be computationally expensive in practice. To alleviate this, early-update methods for structured perceptrons propose an inexact oracle based on beam search, updating the perceptron weights immediately after some number of iterations with a differentiable objective value computation, rather than waiting for the full inference (Collins and Roark, 2004). This popular heuristic has had significant empirical success, but there is currently a lack of theoretical justification for such a choice. Moreover, its relationship to the classical structured perceptron is unclear. For inexact inference methods like beam search to achieve the same guarantees as exact supervised updates, it is essential to develop a deeper theoretical understanding of how these approximations affect convergence properties. Specifically, statements about the ability to learn uniformly over the instance space call for the well-definedness of learning criteria with reduced but aligned implication and constraints. To answer this need and provide increased efficiency, we propose a new algebraic framework, violation-fixing perceptrons, which allows efficient learning over computationally expensive inference procedures through the idea that we should approximate the solution space through solving alternative well-defined free selections. We then need to show that these methods can efficiently generate the feasible prediction target needed for particular piecewise inference-based distributions through the apportioning of group items for tractable uniform optimization. In this paper, we describe a first-generalized violation-fixing perceptron based on updates sourced from inexact computation through inaccuracy events, permutations of choices in a beam or "violations."

With the advent of data-driven approaches, statistical models have proven to be highly effective in capturing the underlying distributions of language, allowing for group translation tasks that gift better results than rule-based approaches. However, despite these successes, translating from one language to another is a multimodal process involving a combinatorial explosion of choices, presenting a perplexing challenge for statistical models. Analysis of Linguistic Style Accommodation in Online Debates In today's digitally intertwined world, the way we communicate has undergone a profound transformation. The proliferation of social media and online platforms has enabled individuals from diverse backgrounds to engage in discussions, debates, and dialogs on an unprecedented scale. As a result, the study of psycholinguistic phenomena, particularly those related to communication and accommodation, has gained significant attention in the fields of linguistics, psychology, information science, and communication theory. One such phenomenon, linguistic style accommodation, has been identified as a crucial element in shaping our understanding of communication and its intricacies. This concept, first introduced by Giles et al. (1991), posits that individuals tend to modify their language styles to accommodate or align themselves with their conversation partners, in an effort to enhance social closeness, reduce intergroup conflict, or convey desired impressions. In the context of online debates, the linguistic style accommodation phenomenon manifests in a unique and intriguing manner. Debates, by their very nature, involve individuals with differing opinions and perspectives engaging in a dynamic and often contentious exchange of ideas. This environment, conducive to linguistic variation and adaptation, presents an ideal setting for studying communication accommodation. On the other hand, various studies have demonstrated that online communication, characterized by its anonymity and mediation through digital interfaces, can often lead to different language styles and accommodations compared to face-to-face interactions. Research has examined linguistic styles and accommodations in various domains, including gesture, linguistics, backchannels, and social media platforms such as tweets (Beebe & Giles, 1984; Coupland, 2007; Giles et al., 1991; Leitner, 2004). These studies have collectively contributed to our understanding of how individuals adjust their language styles to suit specific contexts, others' expectations, or simply to achieve communication efficiency. However, a comprehensive analysis of the linguistic style accommodation phenomenon in online debates has yet to be comprehensively explored. This lacuna is doubly surprising, given the current trend towards online engagements and interactions. Hence, the following paper aims to contribute to this knowledge gap by focusing on the phenomenon within the unique context of online debates. The primary objective of this research is threefold. Firstly, to develop and apply a novel Joint Topic Expression (JTE) model to accurately model debate posts and create a specialized dataset for analyzing linguistic style accommodation in debates. Efficient CCG Parsing: A  versus Adaptive Supertagging Introduction The efficient parsing of Combinatory Categorial Grammar (CCG) remains a crucial yet daunting task in the field of Natural Language Processing (NLP). CCG, a formalism that has gained popularity in the parsing community due to its expressiveness and group lexicalization capabilities, presents a significant challenge when it comes to parsing efficiency. With the growing demand for fast and accurate parsing capabilities in NLP applications, researchers have been exploring various techniques to optimize CCG parsing. In this work, we delve into two orthogonal techniques that have the potential to significantly improve the efficiency of CCG parsing: A  search and adaptive supertagging. A  search, a well-known depth-first search algorithm, has been extensively employed in various problem domains, including AI planning and path finding. Its ability to prune the search space using an admissible heuristic function makes A  particularly appealing for applications where the search space is immense. Despite its effectiveness in other domains, A  has largely remained unexplored in the context of more expressive grammar formalisms, such as CCG. In this paper, we present a thorough evaluation of various A  variants on CCG parsing, demonstrating its potential in reducing parser effort as measured by the number of edges considered during parsing. Adaptive supertagging, on the other hand, has gained popularity as a fast and efficient technique for approximate CCG parsing. By relying on a separate sequence model to prune most lexical categories from the parser's search space, adaptive supertagging effectively reduces the search complexity of CCG parsing without incurring significant losses in parsing accuracy. Its widespread adoption in recent years highlights the need for a systematic comparison and understanding of the strengths and limitations of this technique. Our paper presents a comprehensive evaluation of A  and adaptive supertagging on CCG parsing, considering both hardware-independent measures of parser effort and a more stringent metric of CPU time. By combining the strengths of these two techniques, we explore the possibility of achieving significant improvements in parsing efficiency. The contributions of this work can be summarized as follows: 1) a thorough evaluation of A  search on CCG parsing, including its variant implementations and the impact of different heuristic functions on parsing performance; 2) a systematic comparison of adaptive supertagging with A  search, highlighting their respective strengths and limitations; and 3) an investigation into the benefits of combining A  with adaptive supertagging to achieve faster parsing throughputs.

Exploiting Conversation Structure in Unsupervised Topic Segmentation for Emails Emails are a ubiquitous form of communication in both personal and professional settings, and as such, managing and organizing large email archives has become an increasingly important task. One key aspect of email management is topic segmentation, which involves grouping emails into meaningful categories or topics that reflect the content of the conversation. This is particularly challenging when dealing with long email threads, where the discussion may span multiple topics or subtopics. Traditional topic segmentation models have been based on lexical information, relying on techniques such as bag-of-words or latent semantic analysis to identify thematic patterns in the data [1]. However, these approaches often fail to account for the relational structure of conversation, where the meaning and relevance of individual messages are shaped by their position and context within the thread [2]. For example, a message may introduce a new topic, respond to a previous message, or build upon an earlier idea. These contextual relationships are essential for understanding the conversational dynamics and are typically lost in traditional topic segmentation models. To overcome these limitations, researchers have explored the use of more sophisticated models, including deep learning approaches that can capture complex patterns in the data [3]. However, these methods often require large amounts of annotated data or supervision, which can be time-consuming and expensive to obtain, particularly for specialized domains such as email conversation analysis. In this work, we set out to investigate the problem of unsupervised topic segmentation in email conversations, with a specific focus on the role of conversation structure in these models. We start by introducing a new corpus of email threads, manually annotated with topics, which provides a benchmark for evaluating the performance of various topic segmentation models. Our corpus is unique in its size and scope, and we demonstrate the value of this resource by evaluating annotator reliability and applying existing models to the data. We also assess the effectiveness of two prominent topic segmentation models, the Lexical Chain Segmenter (LCSeg) and Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA), which have been widely used in text analysis tasks. While these models have been shown to be effective in certain contexts, we show that they are limited in their ability to capture the conversation structure inherent in email threads. We then propose two novel extensions of these models that incorporate conversation structure in a principled way, combining the strengths of lexical analysis with the contextual insights provided by conversation structure.

Introduction Transition-based dependency parsing has emerged as a popular approach in natural language processing (NLP), notably due to its versatility in handling various linguistic structures and its ease of integration with neural network architectures. The fundamental idea underlying transition-based parsing is to break down the parsing process into a sequence of transitions or actions, such as shift, left-arc, and right-arc, applied to a stack and a buffer that represent the input sentence. These operations allow the parser to predict the dependency tree structure by iteratively extracting sub-trees from the buffer and incorporating them into the stack. Recent advancements in deep learning have significantly impacted the performance of transition-based parsers, primarily through the incorporation of neural network architectures to learn complex representation spaces from the input text. Traditional machine learning approaches, such as perceptron and Coco-Wiśniewski (C&W), have long been employed to learn the weights of the parser, but their effectiveness and scalability in learning the parser's representation directly from the data are constrained by the need for hand-crafted features and the inability to model long-range dependencies effectively. Consequently, the performance of such models, while notable, often falls short of the current state-of-the-art achieved by transition-based neural network parsers. Motivated by the success of neural network-based approaches in transition-based parsing and the limitations of traditional machine learning methods in learning complex representations, we explore a novel structured perceptron-based framework that combines the efficacy of neural network architectures with the efficiency and interpretability of perceptron training. Our approach stands on the shoulders of state-of-the-art work in NLP and neural network-based parsing, focusing on the structured perceptron as the final trainable layer. By augmenting the gold corpus with a large number of automatically parsed sentences, we integrate a pre-trained network representation and a structured perceptron-based parser that utilizes beam-search decoding for outputting dependency trees. Our system leverages the compositional nature of neural networks to model the parsing decision process effectively and integrate structured perceptron learning to refine the representations and make accurate predictions for constituent subsets. The resulting model inherits the strength of both neural networks (flexibility, scalability) and perceptron (interpretability, provability), combining strength and regulatory conditions within a well-motivated framework. In the following sections, we present a detailed description of our structured perceptron training method for neural network transition-based parsing, followed by empirical investigations of its efficacy, along with critical ablation analysis that sheds light on the performance of the principal architectural components.

Introduction Semantic similarity between words is a fundamental concept in various disciplines spanning artificial intelligence, natural language processing, cognitive science, and psychology. It plays a pivotal role in determining the semantic meaning of texts, where words possessing similar connotations, context, and meaning are identified as semantically similar. The assessment of semantic similarity is a challenging task that has far-reaching implications in numerous applications, including document clustering, information retrieval, and synonym extraction. Researchers and practitioners alike have proposed sophisticated models and techniques to calculate semantic similarity, each leveraging different aspects of linguistic knowledge and computational methods. Conventional approaches to semantic similarity measurement often rely on manually curated lexical resources, such as WordNet or dictionaries. However, these resources have several limitations. Firstly, they are often biased towards specific linguistic domains, which may not generalize well to other domains. Secondly, they tend to be labor-intensive and time-consuming to maintain, especially with the rapidly evolving nature of language and the emergence of new domains. In an attempt to overcome these limitations, researchers have turned their attention to semi-automatic and automatic methods for lexical acquisition and similarity measurement. Nonetheless, the effectiveness of these methods, particularly those leveraging the wealth of information on the web, remains an open question. This paper contributes to the ongoing discourse by introducing a relational model of semantic similarity based on automatically extracted lexical pattern clusters from web sources. Our approach converges insights from linguistic theory and data mining techniques to discover latent patterns in the web-sourced data that capture the underlying semantic relationships between words. By leveraging the power of machine learning and web-sourced data, our method circumvents some of the limitations inherent in traditional lexical resources, facilitating a more robust and comprehensive representation of semantic similarity. We assert that the application of our proposed method enables significant improvements in the accuracy of semantic similarity measurement and practical applications that rely on this capability. To support our claims, we have undertaken an empirical evaluation of the proposed similarity measure against previously proposed semantic similarity measures on Miller-Charles benchmark dataset and WordSimilarity-353 collection. The results of our evaluation demonstrate that our model not only yields superior performance but also exhibits robustness across diverse linguistic domains. Our findings suggest that the web offers a rich and largely unexploited source of information that, when judiciously mined and harnessed, can serve as a powerful tool for advancing our understanding of semantic similarity and related linguistic phenomena.

Introduction Recommender systems have become an indispensable component of modern e-commerce platforms, aimed at assisting users in discovering products that cater to their preferences. The performance of recommender systems heavily relies on the availability of high-quality user and item data, which, unfortunately, is not always forthcoming. With the proliferation of user-generated content on online platforms, multimodal learning has emerged as a promising approach to leverage the auxiliary information available in multiple modalities such as text, images, and ratings. A key advantage of multimodal learning is its ability to capture complex user preferences by incorporating supplementary details about users and items into the recommendation process. For instance, in the context of product recommendations, a product description can provide valuable information about its features and benefits, complemented by the visual attributes depicted in product images. Despite the merits of multimodal learning, existing approaches often struggle with a critical challenge – the presence of missing or corrupted modalities in the user and item data. This phenomenon, arising from various factors such as missing metadata, noisy labels, or incomplete user-item interactions, can significantly impede the performance of recommendation models. Most existing methods, designed to learn from complete and consistent multimodal data, either directly ignore missing modalities, thereby compromising the representational power of the learned models, or attempt to fill the gaps using simplistic imputation strategies, which may not accurately capture the underlying relationships between modalities. As a result, the impressive gains achieved by multimodal learning are, in many cases, undermined by the inadequacies of existing approaches in handling missing modalities. The cold-start problem, a notorious issue in recommender systems, is also exacerbated by the prevalence of missing data. New users or items, lacking a sufficient history of interactions, are often challenging to recommend products to, as the limited information available is insufficient to inform a tailored recommendation strategy. The ability to learn robust representations from multimodal data, even in the presence of missing modalities, would be crucial in addressing both the cold-start problem and the issue of data sparsity, where users or items have limited interaction histories. This requires developing sophisticated approaches that can effectively learn from incomplete multimodal data, leveraging the relationships between different modalities to inform the recommendation process. In this paper, we propose LRMM, a novel framework that addresses the aforementioned challenges by introducing two key innovations: modality dropout (m-drop) and a multimodal sequential autoencoder (m-auto).

Introduction Text similarity measures are a crucial component of various natural language processing (NLP) tasks, such as plagiarism detection, information ranking, recognition of paraphrases, and textual entailment recognition. As the complexity and scale of NLP applications continue to grow, there is a pressing need to develop more sophisticated and robust similarity measures that can accurately capture the subtle relationships between texts. However, existing similarity measures fall short in fully exploiting the sequential nature of language, which is a fundamental aspect of human communication. For instance, traditional methods such as n-grams and skip-grams rely on segmenting the input texts into discrete units, and computing the overlap between these units. While these methods have proven effective to some extent, they ignore the inherent continuity and sequential dependencies within the texts. As a result, they may struggle to handle similar texts that involve minor rephrasings or rearrangements of the original sentences, or those that exhibit nuanced contextual dependencies that require a more nuanced understanding of the language structure. Deep learning has, in recent years, highlighted the relevance of sequential models in various NLP applications, including natural language generation, translation, and text classification. In particular, advances in recurrent neural networks (RNNs) and transformers have demonstrated impressive performance in capturing long-range dependencies and sequential patterns in language. However, despite these advances, existing similarity measures have yet to fully leverage the power of sequential models. In this paper, we draw inspiration from a surprising source: DNA sequence alignment algorithms. These algorithms represent the sequences of nucleotide bases (A, C, G, and T) as continuous curves, rather than discrete units, and use both the actual position of the bases and sequence matching to compute the similarity value. Building on this idea, we propose a novel text similarity measure, which we call TextFlow. TextFlow represents input text pairs as continuous curves and uses both the actual position of the words and sequence matching to compute the similarity value. Our approach has several key advantages. Firstly, it can capture the sequential dependencies and contextual nuances that are often lost in discrete similarity measures. Secondly, it allows for a more fine-grained comparison of text pairs, revealing subtle differences and similarities that may not be apparent through traditional methods. Finally, TextFlow is computationally efficient and can be easily integrated into various NLP applications, making it a promising candidate for real-world deployment. We evaluate TextFlow on eight different datasets, including paraphrase detection, textual entailment recognition, and ranking relevance.

Semantic Parsing Using Content and Context: A Case Study from Requirements Elicitation Requirements elicitation is a critical stage in software development, where specifications are obtained from stakeholders to define the functional and non-functional requirements of a system. However, the requirements elicitation process often involves large volumes of semi-structured documents, which pose challenges for software developers in capturing the detailed and accurate specifications required to successfully implement the system. The main obstacle is the manual process of deciphering these documents, extracting relevant information, and ensuring consistency in the interpretation and representation of the requirements. The process can be time-consuming, labor-intensive, and error-prone, which may lead to misunderstandings and ultimately affect the quality of the final product. In recent years, natural language processing (NLP) and artificial intelligence (AI) techniques have been explored to automate the process of requirements elicitation and specification analysis. Specifically, the advent of deep learning architectures and the availability of annotated datasets for various text-based applications have opened new avenues for researching semantic parsing. Semantic parsing is an essential component in this direction, as it involves mapping natural language inputs to formal representations that can be understood by machines. The primary goal of semantic parsing is to obtain relevant and unambiguous interpretations of text, which can then be used to generate executable code. A live sequence chart (LSC)-based semantic representation is our target in this research. LSCs are multi-modal visual languages that enable the specification of complex behavioral scenarios, which are essential for defining the requirements of a system. Unlike traditional programming languages, LSCs are designed to facilitate scenario-based programming, allowing developers to describe and verify system behavior using behavioral requirements. The key advantage of this representation is that LSCs can be directly translated into executable code, which significantly reduces the complexity of the software development lifecycle. Moreover, the visual form of LSCs allows developers to effortlessly identify ambiguities and inconsistencies in the requirements, making it easier to rectify issues before progressing with the development of the system. To address the task of semantic parsing for requirements elicitation documents, we propose an architecture that integrates sentence-level and discourse-level processing. Our approach leverages a generative probabilistic framework to analyze and disambiguate individual sentences in context. We investigate the effectiveness of our proposed architecture through a case study, comparing the performance of a sentence-based and discourse-based model in constructing a system that accurately reflects all the static (entities, properties) and dynamic (behavioral scenarios) requirements in the document.

Introduction Automatic summarization systems have become increasingly prevalent in modern text analysis, with applications ranging from news articles to scientific research papers. The primary goal of these systems is to condense lengthy documents into concise summaries that capture the most essential information. However, evaluating the performance of summarization systems remains a challenging task, with humans requiring a significant amount of time and effort to assess the quality of generated summaries. To address this challenge, the Text Analysis Conference (TAC) has designed a scoring system to rank summarization systems based on their ability to produce high-quality summaries. The TAC scoring system calculates a single average score for each summarization system across a collection of document sets. While this approach appears to offer a straightforward way to compare and rank systems, it has several limitations that may not accurately reflect the true performance of a summarization system. In this paper, we investigate the statistical appropriateness of the TAC scoring system and propose an alternative that better distinguishes between human and machine evaluation systems. Our motivation stems from the intuition that the average score may not fully capture the diversity and nuances of summarization performance. For instance, a summarization system that excels in certain document sets may perform poorly in others, resulting in an average score that does not accurately represent its overall abilities. Furthermore, the TAC scoring system does not account for the different evaluation strategies employed by human and machine systems, potentially leading to biased comparisons between the two. Human evaluation systems, which involve expert annotators assessing the quality of summaries, may benefit from the diversity of annotators' perspectives and the subjective nature of human judgment. In contrast, machine systems rely on algorithms and statistical models to evaluate summaries, but their evaluation strategies may not be well-suited to capture the full range of human evaluation criteria. To address these limitations, we propose an alternative ranking system that incorporates a statistical framework to assess the performance of summarization systems. Our frameworkaccounts for the variability in summarization performance across document sets and evaluation strategies, ensuring that the ranking system is more robust and accurate. Specifically, we outline a novel approach that uses a probabilistic model to capture the uncertainty and diversity of summarization performance. This model enables us to compute a comprehensive ranking that distinguishes between human and machine evaluation systems, providing a more nuanced understanding of their strengths and weaknesses. Our proposed ranking system has important implications for the evaluation and development of summarization systems, as it enables researchers and practitioners to more accurately compare and improve the performance of these systems.

Introduction The integration of vision and language is a central goal in the field of artificial intelligence (AI), with the ultimate aim of creating machines that can understand and generate rich and meaningful visual data. For decades, researchers have been working on bridging the gap between these two modalities, with significant advances in recent years particularly in the areas of image and video understanding. However, the study of vision and language is an interdisciplinary field that has been hindered by the availability of a quality and diverse set of datasets. Despite the rapid development of new techniques and methodologies, the design, construction, and evaluation of datasets remain crucial to the advancement of the field. Datasets have been widely recognized as a vital component in the development of AI systems, especially in image and video understanding, which are inherently more challenging due to the nuances and complexity associated with these modalities. The conventional assumption is that, the availability of quality datasets that are designed and evaluated in a manner that encourages exploration and discovery, is a fundamental requirement for achieving robust, accurate and reliable results in vision and language research. In recent years, the availability of datasets has experienced an exponential growth, leading to the emergence of some truly landmark image and video datasets that have revolutionized the understanding of various vision and language based tasks. Today, a plethora of datasets are being used for research purposes, ranging from simple classification tasks, detection, and captioning, to more complex tasks such as question answering, storytelling, and generation, and even some few that relate to visual reasoning and image-text matching. However, despite the existence of a large number of vision and language datasets, the landscape of these datasets remains largely fragmented and opaque. There is a clear lack of a platform for evaluating, characterizing, and offering insights into current datasets in the field of vision and language research. Most researchers tend to either ignore the analysis and evaluation of these datasets or spend a substantial amount of their time creating their own datasets. Moreover, most currently existing datasets lack an evaluation criterion that can provide a clear measure of the dataset's value. The lack of quality metrics and categorization runs the risk of promoting stagnation in the area of research within the community. In this paper, we aim to contribute to this ongoing discussion by providing a set of quality metrics for evaluating current vision and language datasets and categorize them accordingly.

Unsupervised Induction of Tree Substitution Grammars for Dependency Parsing Dependency parsing is a fundamental task in Natural Language Processing (NLP) that has garnered significant attention in recent years due to its importance in various applications, including machine translation, question answering, and text summarization. A key challenge in dependency parsing lies in accurately modeling the syntactic structure of sentences, which is critical for capturing the compositional semantics and nuanced implications of language. Traditional dependency parsing models rely on annotated data, which is often time-consuming and expensive to acquire, especially for languages with limited resources. Inducing a dependency grammar directly from text, therefore, presents a compelling approach, as it eliminates the need for annotated data and enables the discovery of linguistic patterns and structures from raw text. This goal has driven research in computational linguistics for decades, yielding various models that parse sentences into dependency trees. Notable approaches to this task include latent variable models, neural dependency parsers, and constraint-based dependency parsers, all of which have achieved impressive results when supervised with annotated data. However, current state-of-the-art models for unsupervised dependency grammar induction often rely on simplistic models that lack the expressive power to capture the nuances and complexity of language. For instance, many models induce a grammar by either learning a collection of regular expressions to match chunk patterns or operating on morphological facts to induce a small set of coarse-grained production rules. These approaches may provide impressive accuracy on certain datasets, but they fail to model the rich structure and compositional properties that are inherent in human language. In recent years, the development of psycholinguistic models of language processing has shed new light on the way human language is processed. A growing body of research suggests that language processing is fundamentally hierarchical and compositional, with the human brain representing language structures in a highly modularized fashion. This evidence has given rise to the development of tree-like grammars, which consists of nodes and edges that form a hierarchical structure that matches the spatial organization of neural tissue. To better capture the sophisticated structure of language, it is essential to develop unsupervised models that can learn Tree Substitution Grammars (TSGs). This type of grammar has been widely recognized as a well-suited formalism for describing linguistic structures, as it provides a precise way of defining grammatical rules that can be both compositional and hierarchical. Although several prior approaches have introduced shallow TSG models for dependency grammar induction, the distribution of tree-like structures across the input text has not been considered.
