Joint Tokenization and Translation Introduction ------------ Natural language processing (NLP) tasks have witnessed tremendous advances in recent years, with machine translation (MT) emerging as one of the most prominent applications. With the rapid growth of language data and computational resources, neural machine translation (NMT) has become the dominant paradigm in the field. While NMT systems have achieved remarkable success in translating sentences from one language to another, they often rely on tokenization – the process of breaking down text into individual words or subwords – to effectively process linguistic input. However, tokenization is not always a straightforward task, particularly for naturally agglutinative languages like Chinese and Korean. These languages frequently exhibit intricate tokenization patterns, where a single word can be formed by combining multiple subwords or characters in various ways. As a result, tokenization errors can have a ripple effect on translation quality, causing the system to mistranslate and generate absurd results. This issue is exacerbated in cases where the translator is biased towards one specific tokenization of the input text. To overcome this challenge, researchers have employed alternative tokenization strategies, including the use of lattices that provide multiple tokenization options for the NMT system to choose from. Lattices have proven effective in improving translation accuracy by accounting for the ambiguities of tokenization. However, their performance is still limited by their reliance on a predefined tokenization framework. In this work, we aim to further alleviate the tokenization error problem by taking a novel approach that jointly tokenizes and translates the input sequence. The core idea behind our joint tokenization and translation framework is to produce a tokenization of the input text and a translation of the source text into the target language simultaneously. Our approach is based on a sequence-to-sequence model that is optimized to maximize the likelihood of the correct tokenization and translation. By integrating tokenization and translation features within the same framework, we can effectively capture the complex relationships between the linguistic structures of the input and output sequences. This is a crucial step towards resolving the limitations of existing NMT systems that are trained on discrete tokenizations, which often do not accurately reflect the nuances of natural language structure. In the following sections, we provide a detailed overview of our joint tokenization and translation framework, evaluate its performance on two prominent language pairs (Chinese-English and Korean-Chinese), and compare it to several state-of-the-art baseline systems.

Semantic Dependency Parsing of NomBank and PropBank: An Efficient Integrated Approach via a Large-scale Feature Selection The landscape of Natural Language Processing (NLP) has witnessed tremendous progress in recent years, with significant advancements in various tasks such as sentiment analysis, machine translation, and question answering. One of the crucial and challenging tasks in NLP is the semantic role labeling (SRL), which involves the identification of predicates and their corresponding roles in a sentence. SRL is a vital component in various NLP applications, including text analysis, question answering, and even dialogue systems. However, SRL remains a challenging task, especially when it comes to processing complex sentences and dealing with deeply nested semantic relations. The integration of NomBank and PropBank has been a pivotal development in SRL research. NomBank and PropBank are two renowned resources for framed semantic role labeling, which are pre-annotated with roles and their corresponding semantic dependencies. While PropBank focuses on a broader set of predicate-argument structures, NomBank is centered around nominal predicates and their respective roles. However, in most existing SRL systems, these two resources are often treated as separate entities, resulting in a duplicative and time-consuming annotation process. This has led to the development of pipeline SRL systems, which involve a sequential processing of PropBank and NomBank annotations. These systems, although effective, suffer from several limitations, including the lack of contextual information sharing and inefficient use of annotated data. Moreover, as highlighted by previous studies, the performance of these pipeline systems quickly degrades when handling long-distance dependencies and deeply nested semantic relations. To bridge this gap, there is a pressing need for an integrated SRL system that can effectively combine the strengths of both NomBank and PropBank, and efficiently capture the contextual information and semantic dependencies in complex sentences. In this paper, we propose a novel integrated SRL system that leverages the compositional properties of NomBank and PropBank features through a large-scale feature selection procedure. By introducing assistant argument labels and extensively incorporating feature templates, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our system in capturing the intricate semantic relations and roles in sentence structures. In this contribution, we aim to take a significant step forward in solving the challenges posed by the integration of NomBank and PropBank features. In what follows, we outline our proposed method and highlight its key components, including the definitions of the SRL system architecture and our integrated feature selection procedure.

This has sparked a surge of interest in multi-document summarization, an area of NLP research that aims to automatically summarize multiple documents to capture the main ideas and key points. Despite the significant progress made in this field, existing multi-document summarization techniques may not be suitable for constructing news overview articles due to their limitations in handling long articles and complex events. In this paper, we investigate a new task of automatically constructing news overview articles by news synthesis and propose a novel approach based on passage segmentation, ranking, selection, and merging. Our proposed approach addresses the limitations of existing multi-document summarization techniques by incorporating a unique passage selection module that identifies the most crucial passages from a set of news articles.

Introduction Automated Text Scoring (ATS) represents a fundamental shift in the way we assess and evaluate written knowledge and skills. Conventional human marking methods are often labor-intensive, costly, and subjective, making them impractical for large-scale assessments. ATS, on the other hand, offers a promising alternative by leveraging computational power and machine learning techniques to consistently and accurately evaluate texts. However, the primary challenge associated with ATS lies in developing robust predictive features that enable the system to make informed scoring decisions. For several years, the development of effective ATS systems has heavily relied on manual feature engineering by human experts. This process involves the identification of relevant linguistic features, such as part-of-speech tags, named entities, and sentiment indicators, and the subsequent incorporation of these features into the scoring model. While manual feature engineering has yielded satisfactory results, it is often time-consuming, domain-specific, and requires extensive expertise in both machine learning and natural language processing (NLP). One promising approach for overcoming the limitations of manual feature engineering is to employ deep learning techniques, particularly neural networks, in ATS. Neural networks are capable of learning complex, hierarchical representations of text data that can capture subtle nuances in language and context. In this work, we propose a novel approach to ATS based on Long-Short Term Memory (LSTM) networks, which represent a type of Recurrent Neural Network (RNN) particularly well-suited to modeling sequential data with temporal dependencies. Our approach involves training an LSTM network to learn high-dimensional representations of text data, where each document is encoded as a dense vector that captures its underlying meaning and scoring characteristics. The key insight behind our approach is that the LSTM network can automatically identify the most discriminative features of a text, such that these features contribute significantly to the overall score. By leveraging this automatic feature discovery capability, our system can eliminate the need for manual feature engineering and instead rely on the LSTM network to identify the most relevant linguistic features. Furthermore, we aim to develop a more interpretable ATS framework by facilitating the visualization of the regions of the text that the LSTM network has identified as most discriminative. This involves developing a novel method for saliency analysis, which generates heat maps that illustrate the contributions of individual words or phrases to the overall score. By providing insight into the decision-making process of the LSTM network, our visualizations enable assessors to better understand how the system arrived at a particular score.

Introduction Envisioning a machine that can understand the intricacies of a temporal story and predict its ending with uncanny accuracy has sparked significant interest in the Natural Language Processing (NLP) community. The development of sophisticated deep learning models has enabled machines to approach human-like cognition, and the ROC Story Cloze Task (SCT) is a particularly intriguing challenge that has garnered substantial attention in recent years. This task, which requires predicting the ending of a story based on a set of incomplete narrative fragments, demands an in-depth comprehension of narrative structure, thematic development, and, ultimately, the ability to generate coherent and plausible conclusions. While state-of-the-art models have demonstrated impressive performance on a range of NLP tasks, existing approaches to the SCT have typically relied on static representations of text, neglecting the dynamic and context-dependent nature of narrative. In contrast, our proposed multi-attention based neural network (MANN) is specifically designed to capture the evolving relationships between narrative elements, temporal cues, and thematic developments. By incorporating a range of well-designed optimizations, including the Highway Network and concatenated features with embedding representations, MANN is equipped to learn nuanced and context-dependent representations that effectively generalize across disparate narrative contexts. However, as compelling as MANN is in its own right, we have taken the next logical step by extending this framework with external knowledge resources, leveraged from a diverse array of sources. These resources – which encompass a universe of domain-specific knowledge, subtly and finely interwoven throughout the narrative – serve as a critical factor in determining the endgame for a story. By introducing external knowledge into the MANN architecture, we unlock new pathways to insight and prediction, exceeding even the highest state-of-the-art results on the SCT benchmark. What is more, a thorough analysis of a representative subset of the SCT stories enables us to drill down into the key competencies that underpin the outperformance of our model: specifically, we examine the roles played by attention mechanisms, knowledge embedding, and histogram quantification, facilitating a sophisticated understanding of how external knowledge contributes to the narrative closure. Distributional semantic models for the evaluation of disordered language Introduction The evaluation of language skills in individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders, such as autism spectrum disorder (ASD), has long been a topic of interest in clinical and linguistic research. A defining characteristic of language in individuals with ASD is its atypical semantic and pragmatic expression, which often manifests as the use of unusual or unexpected words and phrases. This atypicality is thought to reflect underlying differences in semantic meaning representation and processing, as individuals with ASD tend to exhibit difficulties with abstract thought, theory of mind, and empathy (Frith and Happe, 2005; Tager-Flusberg, 2007). In contrast to other language disorders, such as aphasia, which typically result from Damage to the language centres of the brain, the language difficulties associated with ASD are more nuanced and multifaceted, reflecting not only linguistic, but also cognitive and social deficits (Kasari et al., 2012). As a result, the evaluation of language in individuals with ASD requires a more in-depth and multidimensional assessment, incorporating not only traditional measures of language structure and syntax, but also measures of semantic and pragmatic competence. One promising approach to the evaluation of language in ASD is the use of distributional semantic models (DSMs), which represent word meaning as a function of its co-occurrence patterns in a large corpus of text. DSMs have been successfully applied to a range of NLP tasks, including word sense induction, entity disambiguation, and sentiment analysis (Harris, 1954; Turner, 1986; Barbieri et al., 2014). By leveraging the statistical relationships between words in a language, DSMs provide a unique window into the semantic representation and meaning construction processes that underlie language use in individuals with neurodevelopmental disorders. As an evaluation tool for language development, DSMs possess several key advantages. Firstly, they are highly objective and unbiased, eliminating the need for manual coding or human rater agreement, which can introduce unwanted variability and error. Secondly, they are highly scalable, allowing for the analysis of large datasets with ease and speed. Finally, they provide a fine-grained assessment of language use, capturing the nuances of semantic and pragmatic expression that may be lost in more traditional evaluation methods. In this paper, we propose the use of DSMs for the evaluation of disordered language in children with autism. By leveraging the strengths of DSMs, we aim to develop a novel and highly accurate approach to the identification and quantification of atypical semantic and pragmatic expression in children with ASD.

Introduction Matching sentences is a fundamental problem in Natural Language Processing (NLP), arising in various tasks such as entailment detection, answer sentence selection, and text retrieval. The goal of these tasks is to determine the relevance, semantics, or similarity between two sentences, often grounded in the meaning conveyed by the words and their relationships within each sentence. Current approaches to sentence matching typically operate at a coarse level of granularity, ignoring the complex structure inherent in human language. These approaches can either compare sentences word-by-word, ignoring the compositional meaning, or perform a sentence-level comparison, neglecting the nuanced relationships between words and the hierarchical structure of the sentence. Word-level comparisons can be succinct but fail to grasp the deeper semantic relationships between sentences. On the other hand, sentence-level comparisons often ignore the syntactic and semantic nuances that arise from the internal structure of the sentence. The pre-processing step to obtain the structural alignment between sentences is often non-differentiable and prone to errors in the propagation of inaccuracies. Consequently, the performance of current sentence matching models often falls short of human-like understanding and judgment. However, recent advances in deep learning and transformer-based architectures have opened up new avenues for understanding and modeling complex structures in natural language. In this paper, we delve into the realm of structured alignments to introduce a novel approach for comparing sentences. Our proposed model, called Structured Alignment Networks (SAN), adopts a tree-structured perspective for sentence matching by leveraging a structured attention mechanism. This attention mechanism enables the simultaneous alignment and discovery of the latent tree structure that underlies each sentence. Unlike existing models, SAN does not rely on pre-prosessing steps to obtain sentence structures. Instead, it uses a fully differentiable architecture that learns the structural representations of the input sentences through a self-supervised process. This eliminates the inherent issues of error propagation associated with non-differentiable pre-processing steps. Furthermore, SAN simultaneously matches the candidate spans within the input sentences and discovers the structured relationships between words, capturing the latent tree structure of the sentence. Building upon this structured alignment, SAN provides an efficient and intuitive framework for assessing the semantic relationships between sentences. By encoding the internal structure of each input sentence, our SAN model can differentiate between sentences with superficial similarities yet carry different meanings, as well as those that convey similar meanings through altered phrasing but with no apparent surface-level similarity.

Mine Bilingual Data from the Web with Adaptively Learnt Patterns Introduction The rapid expansion of the web has given rise to an unprecedented amount of multilingual content, significantly contributing to the acquisition of large-scale bilingual datasets. These datasets, encompassing bilingual sentences and terms, have been found to be invaluable for various Natural Language Processing (NLP) applications. Among these applications, machine translation and cross-language information retrieval have drawn considerable attention from the research community due to their potential in facilitating seamless communication across linguistic and cultural boundaries. Currently, several approaches for extracting bilingual data from the web exist, primarily relying on either manual curation or data crawl-based methods, both of which are often limited by the scale of data that can be handled and the duration required for the data collection process. While more efficient algorithms have been proposed, an essential challenge remains—ensuring the accuracy and consistency of the bilingual data collected. In this regard, our work in this paper is motivated by an intriguing observation that bilingual data on the web typically appear in clusters, more often than not, following similar patterns. This insight leads us to propose an innovative, adaptive pattern-based bilingual data mining method. The primary aim of our approach is to establish a more effective and robust framework for collecting high-quality bilingual data, which would in turn play a pivotal role in furthering the capabilities of our NLP applications. To achieve this objective, we set forth a structured four-step methodology. First, the web content is parsed into a Document Object Model (DOM) tree and subsequently segmented to extract substrings—referred to as snippets—and serve as the fundamental units of our analysis. Following this, our approach employs a sophisticated word-based alignment model that considers not only translation but also transliteration factors to identify potential translation pairs, dubbed seeds. Subsequently, these identified seeds are utilized to learn generalized patterns that encompass various types of bilingual data. Finally, the mined bilingual data is extracted based on these learned patterns. Grounded in an empirical evaluation on large-scale Chinese web pages, our proposed method delivers remarkably effective performance. Specifically, it generates more than 7.5 million pairs of bilingual sentences and more than 5 million pairs of bilingual terms, both of which exhibit impressively high accuracy rates—each surpassing 80%. In essence, the development and implementation of this adaptive pattern-based bilingual data mining method constitutes a significant step toward fostering more accurate and efficient extraction of bilingual data, which, in turn, will empower machine translation and cross-language information retrieval applications to better assimilate and utilize the vast, multilingual web resources available

Joint Modeling of Trigger Identification and Event Type Determination in Chinese Event Extraction Event extraction is a crucial task in natural language processing (NLP) that aims to identify and categorize key events or arguments from text. It plays a significant role in various applications, such as question answering, sentiment analysis, and text summarization. In Chinese, the complexity of the language and the lack of high-quality annotated corpora make event extraction more challenging than in European languages. Current Chinese event extraction systems rely heavily on annotated event corpora, which often suffer from noisy data and low annotation quality. Moreover, due to the ambiguity and polysemy of Chinese words, many pseudo trigger mentions are introduced into the event extraction process, hindering the model's performance and interpretability. Traditionally, trigger identification and event type determination are treated as two separate tasks in event extraction. Trigger identification focuses on identifying the words or phrases that function as the core of an event, while event type determination aims to categorize the event into predefined types. However, these two tasks are highly correlated, as the event type can often be inferred from the trigger words, and vice versa. Inspired by the synergy between these two tasks, we propose a joint model of trigger identification and event type determination for Chinese event extraction. Our approach leverages the mutual benefits of these two tasks to improve the performance and robustness of event extraction models. In this paper, we propose a novel joint model that integrates trigger identification and event type determination into a unified framework. Our model is based on a bilevel optimization architecture, where the trigger identification and event type determination are tackled simultaneously through a shared set of features. Specifically, we design a hierarchical architecture with a trigger identification module and an event type determination module. The trigger identification module uses a multi-task learning approach to identify potential trigger words, taking into account contextual and linguistic features. The event type determination module then categorizes the identified triggers into predefined event types, benefiting from the structured knowledge graph of event types. To address the critical issue of pseudo trigger mentions, we also introduce several novel trigger filtering schemas. These schemas exploit various linguistic and semantic features to differentiate between true triggers and pseudo triggers. By combining these trigger filtering schemas with the joint model, we can effectively filter out pseudo trigger mentions and improve the reliability of event extraction results.

Introduction Machine translation (MT) has made tremendous strides in recent years with the advent of deep learning techniques. Modern MT systems have achieved state-of-the-art performance in various languages, including those with low resource availability. However, a single MT system often fails to capture the nuances of human language and nuances, and hence, system combination has been widely adopted as a promising technique to overcome these limitations. By aggregating the outputs from multiple MT systems, system combination aims to produce a more accurate and fluent translation. Confusion network decoding, proposed by Brill and Wu (2000), has shown impressive performance gains in combining MT system outputs. This approach models the hypotheses from different MT systems as a confusion network where each node represents a possible translation. By traversing the confusion network, the most likely and feasible translation path is determined. However, one major challenge that hinders the performance of confusion network decoding is the alignment of hypotheses from multiple systems. Hypothesis alignment refers to mapping the words between different translations into their corresponding positions, which is more challenging than hypothetical word alignment for document-level machine translation, since the word order may significantly differ between the translation pairs. To address this issue, various word alignment methods have been proposed, including GIZA++ (Och and Ney, 2003), TER (Snover et al., 2004), CLA (Koehn and Hoang, 2007) and IHMM (Constant et al., 2006). Each of these methods has its unique strengths and weaknesses, such as handling long-distance dependencies and modeling ambiguity between different alignments. However, there lacks a systematic study comparing their performances for improving the reliability of hypothesis alignment in the context of MT system combination. Moreover, almost all previous studies that utilize multiple alignment techniques solely rely on a single word alignment to form the confusion network, which may dilute the effectiveness of the combination. In this paper, we aim to fill these gaps by conducting an extensive evaluation of the four most frequently used word alignment methods (GIZA++, TER, CLA and IHMM) for hypothesis alignment in confusion network-based MT system combination. Furthermore, we propose a more robust approach, namely the intersection word alignment, which integrates both direct and inverse word alignment to strengthen the confidence of hypothesis alignment. Our results demonstrate that this intersection word alignment method not only yields consistent performance improvement over the state-of-the-art word alignment techniques but also produces a more accurate confusion network.

Introduction Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has become a vital technology in natural language processing, enabling efficient and accurate translation of text from source languages to target languages. The training of SMT models relies heavily on bilingual corpora, which are often comprised of parallel text in multiple languages simultaneously. Given the rapidly increasing demand for language translation services in a multilingual world, developing and adapting SMT models to support diverse languages has become an essential research direction. In modern translation scenarios, languages do not exist in isolation, and a certain level of linguistic similarity is expected across different languages, often facilitating processes such as lexicosediment and data enrichment. The multilingual approach takes advantage of this similarity by using parallel corpora that span multiple languages. By exploiting shared linguistic features, multilingual models can leverage knowledge across languages to handle similar translation tasks more accurately and generalizable than their monolingual counterparts. One significant challenge in developing effective and efficient multilingual SMT models lies in data acquisition and updating. Specifically, adding new languages to an existing multilingual SMT model necessitates in-depth analysis and selection of high-quality parallel text, which can be time-consuming and resource-intensive. Moreover, training models on relevant language pairs often require a heavy upfront effort in collecting and aligning parallel text data. Active learning (AL) has recently emerged as a promising solution for mitigating these challenges. AL is a subset of supervised learning that focuses on dynamically selecting the most informative instances from the training set with the goal of reducing the number of annotations required during the training process. This has been extremely beneficial in applications such as text classification, recommendation systems, computer-aided design and more. By judiciously selecting a subset of relevant examples from a large corpus that needs to be labeled by a human annotator and then incorporating these labels into the training set, AL can yield comparable or even superior results to a fully labeled dataset, while also significantly reducing the amount of human effort needed. In the context of multilingual SMT, applying AL techniques can provide a unique opportunity to improve language coverage without the need for large-scale parallel text gathering and processing. Our work focuses on introducing a novel active learning task specifically designed for enriching high-quality multilingual translation systems by leveraging the EuroParl corpus, and evaluates various efficient sentence selection methods to identify the most effective heuristics for this purpose.

While this has proven effective in various NLP systems, little attention has been paid to exploring the potential complementarity between parsing and semantic role labeling. The dominance of this unidirectional pipeline has also resulted in limited understanding of how a parser might benefit from information provided by a semantic role labeler. In this paper, we take a systematic and constructive approach to rectify this oversight by designing a novel system that enables bidirectional information flow between a parser and a semantic role labeler. By bringing semantic role predictions into the parsing process, we demonstrate that it is possible to improve the overall performance of the system. Concretely, our system distinguishes likely from unlikely semantic roles using an averaged perceptron model, and it penalizes parses that give rise to low-scoring semantic roles. This new parsing process gives primacy to theoretically optimal parses based on their potential to accurately facilitate meaning representation and interpretation. In the first experiment, we use a baseline generative model to produce a set of n-best parses, which we then re-order using our semantic model. Introduction Information retrieval (IR) has long been a fundamental problem in the field of natural language processing, with applications in search engines, text classification, and information retrieval systems. Traditional information retrieval models, such as bag-of-words (BoW) models, rely on term frequencies and document frequencies to rank documents in response to a query. While these models have shown impressive results in various tasks, they fall short in capturing nuanced similarities among terms and their semantic relationships. Recent advances in natural language processing have led to the development of various neural IR models, which utilize neural networks to model the semantic relationships between terms and documents. However, traditional neural IR models often lack the interpretability and scalability of traditional BoW-based models, making it challenging to implement and maintain large-scale information retrieval systems. Furthermore, many neural IR models rely on manual feature engineering, which can be time-consuming and prone to overfitting. In this paper, we propose a novel probabilistic framework for information retrieval, which leverages the power of hierarchical Dirichlet trees (HDTs) to capture similarities among terms. HDTs offer a flexible and structured way to represent the vocabulary, allowing for the capture of linguistic relationships and semantic dependencies between terms. By modeling the term vocabulary as a hierarchical tree, we can effectively represent the distribution of terms in a document and retrieve documents based on occurrences of specific query terms, as well as similarities between terms. This effect is similar to query expansion, which enhances the precision of search results by automatically generating a set of related terms to the original query. The use of HDTs in information retrieval offers several advantages over traditional BoW-based models and neural IR models. Firstly, HDTs exhibit an effect similar to inverse document frequency (IDF), which reduces the importance of common terms and amplifies the importance of rare terms in the document collection. Hidden Softmax Sequence Model for Dialogue Structure Analysis Introduction Dialogue allows humans to communicate with each other in a more expressible and understandable manner. In order to develop more natural and user-friendly artificial intelligence (AI) systems, understanding the structure of conversations is a fundamental problem in the field of natural language processing (NLP). Dialogue structure analysis is a computer science task aimed at studying the patterns of conversations to generate meaningful and human-like responses. Existing approaches to dialogue structure analysis generally rely on supervised learning models, such as conditional random fields (CRFs) and long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, which require manually annotated dialogue data for training. However, the annotation process is time-consuming, expensive, and often unavailable. Furthermore, supervised learning models tend to capture domain specific patterns and therefore lack generalizability to new domains. To tackle this challenge, unsupervised learning approaches, which can learn from raw data without any manual annotations, have become increasingly popular in recent years. Unsupervised learning has already shown promising results in various tasks, such as machine translation and document topic modeling. Nonetheless, the application of unsupervised learning to dialogue structure analysis is still in its infancy. Inspired by the success of unsupervised learning in various tasks, we delve into the realm of dialogue structure analysis and explore the feasibility of unsupervised learning in this domain. Our primary motivation is to devise an unsupervised learning framework for dialogue structure analysis that can capture both local and global patterns in conversations. Specifically, we aim to discover hidden states of utterances, latent topics specified by dialogues, and the global topic shared across the whole dialogue corpus in an unified and systematic manner. To this end, we propose a novel supervised modeling method that integrities a family of nonlinear functions and a probabilistic graphical model to infer these dialogue structures. To gauge the efficacy of our proposed framework, we perform an extensive comparison of our model with several state-of-the-art supervised and unsupervised models on two large-scale real-world dialogue corpora, Twitter-Posts and AirTicketBooking. The experimental results demonstrate that our model significantly outperforms the competing models on a range of evaluation metrics, highlighting its superiority in capturing dialogue structures. The contributions of this work can be summarized as follows. Firstly, we propose a novel unsupervised learning model, the hidden softmax sequence model (HSSM), for dialogue structure analysis. Our model captures both the dependency between latent states and the global topic shared across the whole dialogue corpus.

Unsupervised Neural Dependency Parsing Dependency parsing is a fundamental task in natural language processing that aims to uncover the grammatical structure of a sentence by identifying the relationships between words and their dependents. Among various parsing paradigms, dependency parsing has emerged as a popular choice due to its clear and intuitive representation of sentence structure. Traditional dependency parsing techniques rely heavily on hand-engineered features and rule-based approaches to capture the complex relationships between words. However, these methods often struggle to generalize across languages and contexts, as the design of features and rules can be highly language-dependent and demand significant expert knowledge. In recent years, the rise of deep learning models, particularly neural networks, has transformed the field of natural language processing, offering a promising avenue for improving unsupervised dependency parsing. These models have shown remarkable ability to handle complex linguistic phenomena and adapt to diverse language families. Incorporating neural networks into the unsupervised dependency parsing paradigm can take advantage of their powerful feature learning capabilities, potentially leading to more robust and generalizable models. One key challenge in this direction is how to effectively inject prior knowledge, often in the form of linguistic rules or features, into the neural network architecture to ensure that the model adheres to the structural properties of natural languages. In particular, there exists a myriad of correlations and patterns in the parameters of grammar rules that elucidate the relationships between different Parts-of-Speech (POS) tags. However, previous methods dealing with such information have shown limitations, employing either ad-hoc feature designs or sophisticated prior distributions that exhibit poor interpretability and may not generalize to diverse data distributions. Given the shortcomings of these methods, there is a pressing need for novel approaches that can effectively capture the complexities of dependency grammar from POS tags in an unsupervised setting. This requires the ability to learn a distributed representation of POS tags, encoding the interdependencies and correlations between different tags, without relying on the expert knowledge of human designers. Learning such a representation offers several advantages over existing hand-engineered feature approaches: it is adaptive, generalizable to unobserved POS tags, and can more effectively tease out complex relationships between POS tags and dependency grammar. In this paper, we propose a neural network-based approach to unsupervised dependency parsing that obviates the need for manually crafted features and prior knowledge by using a self-regularized architecture to predict grammar rule probabilities based on the distributed representation of POS tags.

Neural Machine Translation via Binary Code Prediction Introduction The impressive advances in neural machine translation (NMT) have made it a state-of-the-art approach for translating natural languages, outperforming traditional statistical machine translation methods in many language pairs. A key component of NMT systems is the output layer, which is responsible for predicting the next word in a sequence given the preceding words. This task is daunting, especially when dealing with large vocabulary sizes found in most natural languages. The standard approach to achieve this is through the use of a softmax function, which computes the probability distribution over all possible words and selects the one with the highest probability. However, the computation required by the softmax function grows linearly with the vocabulary size, making it impractical for large vocabularies and imposing substantial memory and computational requirements. There have been attempts to alleviate this issue using alternative formulations, such as normalized importance sampling, or actor-critic reinforcement learning-based methods. Nevertheless, these approaches do not always offer substantial advantages in memory and computational efficiency. In this paper, we explore an alternative approach to calculate the output layer, which is inspired by information theory and computer science. The idea is to predict a binary code for each word, rather than a probability distribution over the vocabulary. By leveraging properties of binary codes, we demonstrate that this approach can dramatically reduce the computational memory requirements and decoding speed of the output layer in NMT systems. Our proposed method for generating binary codes draws from the theoretical foundations of error-correcting codes. These codes are designed to quickly and efficiently recover the original data from a corrupted version, which occurs when the bits are flipped in a random pattern. This insight can be utilized in the context of NMT to predict a binary code representing the target word, rather than a probability distribution. By doing so, we can latch onto the robust properties of error-correcting codes to gain a significant reduction in the computation and memory requirements of the output layer. Another critical aspect of NMT systems is ensuring that the predicted binary codes indeed represent the correct word. This requires developing novel techniques to adapt the trained model so that it can recover the original word (correct the binary code) in the event of an error. In order to resolve this challenge, we need to introduce alternative methods and blend conventional softmax prediction with binary codes.

Denoising Distantly Supervised Open-Domain Question Answering Introduction: The rapid growth of unstructured text data has sparked significant interest in open-domain question answering (OD-QA), a task that aims to find answers from an extensive collection of unlabeled text. Traditional question answering models rely heavily on supervised learning, where each question is manually annotated with its corresponding answer and context, making the process labor-intensive and often impractical. To mitigate this limitation, distant supervision (DS) has emerged as a promising approach, utilizing large-scale, unlabeled text corpora to indirectly supervise model training. By leveraging the natural language and data abundance available in these corpora, DS can scale effectively with minimal human effort. Distantly supervised open-domain question answering (DS-QA) builds on this concept by extending the scope of supervised learning from simple retrieval tasks to full-fledged question answering. Prior DS-QA models focus primarily on retrieving the most relevant paragraph for each question, ignoring valuable information potentially hidden within other paragraphs. This narrow approach neglects the hypothetical "coverage" in DS-QA, leaving the possibility for relevant information, including the answer, to be buried amidst numerous paragraphs. Another crucial challenge associated with DS-QA is the inevitable problem of noisy labeling in the supervision data. Due to the lack of human-annotated ground truth, DS models can easily fall prey to mislabeled examples. These noisy examples not only fail to contribute to the overall accuracy of the model but also introduce biases and negative impacts on the performance of these models. Consequently, there is a pressing need for a DS-QA framework that can mitigates noise in the data to ensure the high-quality performance of the model. Recent breakthroughs in modeling architectures and training methodologies have opened up new avenues for alleviating these shortcomings. This paper proposes a novel, innovative DS-QA model that tackles both issues: the "coverage" problem and the noisy labeling problem. Our proposed model introduces a paragraph selector to purposefully eliminate those noisy and less relevant paragraphs, thus reducing the data noise, thereby augmenting the accuracy of trained DS-QA models. Concurrently, it proposes a paragraph reader that plaintively extracts the correct answer from the filtered paragraphs, bringing out the best possible performance. By reconciling these two ages of improvements, we aim to achieve a more robust and accurate DS-QA model, yielding significant improvements over existing state-of-the-art baselines. In the following sections, we delves into the architectural details of our proposed DS-QA model and report on the striking results that deservingly underscore the contributions of our work.

Exploiting Bilingual Information to Improve Web Search The phenomenon of globalization has led to a multilingual online landscape, where searchers from diverse linguistic and cultural backgrounds access the same information on the web. This diversity poses challenges to search engines, which must provide accurate and relevant results to users across different languages and regions. Despite the widespread use of group queries in English and other languages, existing search engines largely neglect the linguistic diversity of the web. Consequently, the quality of search results often varies across languages, with the same information need returning vastly different rankings even within the same search engine. In recent years, there has been a notable shift in the approach to web search, towards more sophisticated models that incorporate user behavior, context, and relevance. However, the development of domain-independent ranking models remains an open challenge. One key problem is that these models often fail to capture language-specific nuances, leading to mismatches in relevance and recalls for non-English searchers. In this paper, we investigate the idea of exploiting bilingual information to improve web search efficiency and accuracy by learning a ranking function on bilingual queries. Our approach focuses on using pairs of documents from different languages to train a unified ranking model, thereby leveraging language-specific cues to generalize better across various languages and linguistic communities. By proposing a bilingual ranking technique that combines both monolingual and bilingual features, our model can optimize the ranking of similar but linguistically-distinct content. This hybrid approach is motivated by the notion that bilingual queries represent equivalent search intentions, providing insights into the interdependence of document relevance and language. Our method relies on bilingual data augmentation, leveraging the availability of cross-language query logs to generate relevant pairs of monolingual documents from a target language. Through collaborative supervised modeling, our proposed system is designed to balance the relative weights between monolingual and bilingual features to form a generalized ranking function. The testing framework of our proposed bilingual ranking model involves evaluating the ranking technique on both English and Chinese query logs and measuring its performance relative to that of a highly competitive monolingual ranking algorithm. Our results, derived from experiments conducted on publicly available datasets, demonstrate that our proposal significantly outperforms prior ranking methods by more than 26% and 18% respectively for English and Chinese languages. Moreover, our method offers impressive sensitivity to language parity, highlighting the value offered by bilingual enrichment in this context.

Towards Implicit Content-Introducing for Generative Short-Text Conversation Systems Introduction: The rapid advancement of human-computer conversation systems has attracted substantial attention from researchers in the field of artificial intelligence. Among various approaches to build these systems, generative Sequence-to-Sequence (Seq2Seq) models have emerged as a particularly popular choice, allowing the system to engage in conversation by generating responses based on the input question or prompt. These models leverage the power of neural networks to learn the underlying patterns and relationships in language, thereby facilitating the generation of coherent and meaningful responses. However, despite their potential, standard Seq2Seq models are often plagued by the limitation of generating trivial or uninformative replies, particularly in short-text conversation settings. This phenomenon is largely attributed to the model's reliance on a fixed vocabulary and the absence of an explicit mechanism for introducing relevant information into the response. As a result, the system may fail to capture the nuances of the conversation and provide meaningful feedback to the user. For instance, when responding to a question about a specific topic, the model might simply repeat a few related words or phrases without providing any additional context or insight. This can lead to an unsatisfying conversation experience and undermine the trust and confidence placed in the system. To address this issue, our research focuses on developing an implicit content-introducing method for generative short-text conversation systems. The underlying idea is to incorporate additional information into the Seq2Seq model in a flexible and seamless manner, allowing it to generate more meaningful and informative replies. Our approach involves introducing auxiliary cue words into the decoding process, which are then fused with the general decoding information using a hierarchical gated fusion unit. This unit is designed to selectively weigh the contributions of the general decoding and cue word information, ensuring that the final response is both coherent and relevant to the conversation topic. By incorporating this implicit content-introducing mechanism into the Seq2Seq model, we aim to enhance the overall performance of the conversational system and improve the user experience. Our proposed method is evaluated on real-life data, and the results demonstrate significant improvements over a set of competitive baselines in terms of BLEU scores and human evaluation. This study contributes to the ongoing research in human-computer conversation systems and provides a novel solution to the challenge of generating informative responses in short-text conversation settings.

Introduction The rapid growth of machine learning and artificial intelligence has led to significant advancements in natural language generation, with applications in various domains, such as customer service, news summaries, and data-to-text generation. Data-to-text generation, in particular, is a critical task that involves generating descriptive texts based on a set of database records. This process has far-reaching implications in fields like data analytics, customer support, and decision-making. With the widespread availability of large datasets and sophisticated neural architectures, recent models have made substantial progress in this task, achieving state-of-the-art results on several well-established benchmarks. Nevertheless, despite the remarkable advancements, data-to-text models still face the significant challenge of ensuring the precision of data records in the generated texts. The limitations of current data-to-text models are particularly evident in complex and realistic scenarios, such as those presented by the ROTOWIRE dataset. ROTOWIRE is a challenging benchmark that requires the generation of sports-related news articles based on input data records, including player statistics, team performances, and game outcomes. The task demands not only accurate data representation but also coherent, engaging, and relevant information, making it an exemplary test-bed for assessing the precision and overall quality of generated texts. In particular, the problem of inaccurate data records in generated texts is a pressing concern for several reasons. Firstly, incorrect information can compromise the reliability and trustworthiness of the generated texts, which can have severe consequences in critical applications like financial reporting, legal documentation, and healthcare communication. Secondly, the propagation of errors can quickly escalate, rendering the entire system ineffective and potentially causing further errors or even perpetuating misinformation. To address these challenges, this paper proposes a novel two-stage approach, dubbed "Point Precisely," which leverages a delayed copy mechanism to enhance the precision of data records in generated texts. Unlike traditional models that integrate copying and generating mechanisms uniformly throughout the decoding process, our delayed copy mechanism decouples the two components into two separate stages: template generation and data slot filling. This architecture allows our model to first generate a high-quality template text with data slots to be filled, followed by a deliberate and informed process of copying data records into these slots. By decoupling these stages, we provide a more nuanced control over the generation process, enabling our model to generate more accurate and informative texts. Our proposed delayed copy mechanism is equipped with double attention, position-aware attention, and a pairwise ranking loss, which enable the model to take into account the full context of input data records and generated templates.

Introduction Probabilistic Context-Free Grammars (PCFGs) have been a cornerstone of Natural Language Processing (NLP) for several decades, and their ability to efficiently capture structural regularities in language has made them a popular choice for a wide range of applications, including parsing, machine translation, and language modeling. However, the reliability and effectiveness of PCFGs heavily depend on accurate parameter estimation from a large and diverse set of training data. One of the major challenges in learning PCFG models is handling the complex distribution over tree spaces, which is not easily tractable due to the vast number of possible trees of a given size. This difficulty, coupled with the latent nature of some PCFG applications, has impeded the development of provably correct and efficient learning algorithms for such models. Latent-variable PCFGs, in particular, impose an additional layer of complexity by requiring the estimation of unobservable variables, such as the latent categories or co-occurrence relationships between syntactic and lexical attributes of a tree. Traditional approaches to learning PCFG models often rely on ad-hoc, maximum-likelihood-based parameter estimation, which can lead to suboptimal results, especially when dealing with limited training data or heavily variable linguistic phenomena. Furthermore, the risk of overfitting and underfitting remains a persistent problem, rendering the choice of hyperparameters as a crucial yet empirical task in model development. In this work, we focus on developing a learning algorithm for latent-variable PCFGs that is both provably correct and computationally efficient. To achieve this, we integrate two key components: a matrix-decomposition algorithm applied to a co-occurrence matrix estimated from parse trees in a training sample, and the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm applied to a convex objective derived from the training samples in combination with the output from the matrix decomposition. Our method addresses both the estimation of latent variables and the efficient handling of the tree space through a novel and structured approach. We conduct experiments on both parsing and a language modeling problem to demonstrate the applicability and effectiveness of our algorithm in practice. By providing a reliable learning framework for latent-variable PCFGs, we expect our work to have a significant impact on the development of NLP models that can accurately capture and exploit structural regularities of natural language. By improving the theoretical foundations and algorithmic design of PCFG learning, our work also contributes to the broader goal of building more robust and data-efficient NLP systems that can generalize better to under-resourced or unseen linguistic phenomena.

Morphology, as a subfield of linguistics, studies the internal structure of words and how they are formed from smaller units called morphemes. Inflectional morphology, in particular, deals with the various ways in which words change form to express different grammatical functions, such as tense, number, and case. Accurately identifying and modeling morphological patterns has been a long-standing challenge in natural language processing (NLP), as it underlies numerous applications, including language modeling, machine translation, and text analysis. Traditional approaches to morphological paradigm learning have primarily relied on rule-based processes and probabilistic models, such as data-driven methods based on Hidden Markov models (HMMs) or transformation-based error-driven learning. However, these approaches can be computationally expensive and often lack transparency in the learned representations. Recently, a simple yet competitive strategy for inducing morphological patterns has been proposed by leveraging the longest common subsequence (LCS) found in inflection tables. This non-probabilistic strategy has been shown to effectively capture morphological regularities in various languages. One key challenge in utilizing the LCS-based strategy is extending it to cover the entire range of morphological possibilities relevant to unseen words, especially for languages with complex paradigms or limited labeled data. To this end, we propose a novel framework that integrates the LCS-based strategy with discriminative classification techniques. Our system has two primary components: the first is responsible for learning morphological paradigms from labeled examples of inflection patterns (inflection tables), while the second component uses a trained classifier to predict inflection tables for unseen lemmas or base forms. The integration of the LCS strategy with discriminative classification is crucial for enabling our system to efficiently learn and generate complete inflection tables for unseen words. By explicitly modeling the relationship between inflection tables and morphological paradigms, our system can effectively reconstruct accurate inflection tables even for words that have not been seen during training. This is made possible by leveraging the highly regularized structure of morphological paradigms, which provides a strong foundation for discriminative classification. In this paper, we provide an in-depth exploration of our proposed framework, which combines the LCS-based strategy for inflection table generalization with a discriminative classifier. We evaluate the performance of our system on a diverse set of datasets covering 11 languages, with the aim of demonstrating its effectiveness in learning and generating high-accuracy morphological resources. Our experiments indicate that this integrated approach yields consistently higher accuracies compared to other methods on the same task, thus pointing to the potential of the general methodology as a viable approach for quickly creating high-accuracy morphological resources.

Improved Semantic Representations From Tree-Structured Long Short-Term Memory Networks Introduction: Recent years have witnessed a surge in the development and deployment of Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs) for sequence modeling tasks. Among these, Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks have emerged as a popular and highly effective approach for preserving temporal dependencies in sequential data. However, the majority of LSTM-related research has focused on exploiting linear chain-based network architectures, which, although highly efficient, are often found to be less effective at capturing the intricate syntactic properties present in natural language. In order to reduce the gap between the linear chain-based LSTM and the more complex syntactic properties of natural language, we must consider more sophisticated network architectures, which not only more effectively capture temporal dependencies but also inculcate the syntactic and structural properties of language, including the way words combine to form phrases and sentences. Inspired by this necessity, we must generalize the linear chain-based LSTM structure, avoiding the flaws that have been revealed and incorporating certain features intrinsic to natural language. In the following sections, we will delve deeper into the details of our proposed tree-structured LSTM architecture, its constituent components and how it compares to existing systems in terms of its ability to generalize sequence modeling problems.

Word Maturity: Computational Modeling of Word Knowledge Introduction In natural language processing, estimating word difficulty is a crucial task that has numerous applications in educational and assessment settings. The difficulty of words in a lexical database can be estimated using various computational methods, with a general goal of providing an indication of how challenging a word might be for a learner to understand or acquire. However, the majority of these methods rely on scalar approaches, where each word is assigned a single level of difficulty along a hypothetical scale. This oversimplification overlooks the fact that word knowledge does not unfold in a linear fashion. Rather, learners accumulate knowledge incrementally at multiple stages of language acquisition. Traditional corpus-based methods for estimating word difficulty, such as frequency-based metrics or part-of-speech-based metrics, are inherently deficient in capturing this complex progression. These methods tend to rely on word-level characteristics, like frequency, length, or part-of-speech, and are prone to over-simplifying the nuanced nature of language acquisition. Moreover, such metrics typically neglect social and contextual factors that play a critical role in language learning, such as domain knowledge, cultural background, and situational awareness. Researchers have acknowledged the limitations of scalar approaches and corpus-based methods, but propose various adaptations instead of departing from the traditional methods. New approaches include multi-level modeling for capturing morphological complexity (Krakovsky et al., 2017) and psycholinguistic-inspired metrics (Habib et al., 2016). However, even these novel approaches differ from our outlined solutions by focusing on narrower issues of language learning and provide only minor improvements in capturing the true complexity of word difficulty. To transcend the inherent limitations of these approaches, our research proposes a fresh perspective on word difficulty estimation, namely Word Maturity (WM). Our key idea is to move beyond scalar representations and instead, model word knowledge as an evolving construct that escalates developmentally across the acquisition sequence. WM emphasizes the dynamic progression of word knowledge, an understanding of which is accessible through computational modeling. By leveraging Latent Semantic Analysis, we can efficiently create a more faithful model of language learning, offering predictions and explanations that are grounded in deep linguistic properties. To demonstrate the viability of WM, this study presents a novel computational algorithm that generates an explicit and continuous ages of maturity for each word in the lexicon. Our algorithm deflects the prevalent scalar evaluations of word difficulty by fostering a greater understanding of the relationships between the distribution of words in different domains, levels of language expertise and language processing complexities.

A Coherence Model Based on Syntactic Patterns Introduction The study of coherence in text has been a long-standing challenge in the field of natural language processing (NLP) and computational linguistics. Coherence refers to the way in which multiple sentences or clauses in a passage interconnect and contribute to the overall flow of meaning [1]. Identifying coherent text is crucial in various applications, such as text summarization, question answering, and sentiment analysis, where the ability to accurately distinguish between coherent and incoherent text is essential for achieving good performance. However, current methods for assessing coherence primarily rely on shallow lexical or semantic analysis [2], which often fails to capture the underlying intentional structure of text. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to modeling coherence that leverages syntactic patterns in text. Our hypothesis is that syntax serves as a proxy for the communicative goal of a sentence and, as such, the sequence of sentences in a coherent discourse should exhibit detectable structural patterns. This idea is rooted in the idea that certain syntactic configurations are more likely to convey a particular message or contribute to a specific purpose in a text. For instance, a sentence sequence consisting of causal or comparative clauses often suggests a more logical and connected flow of information. By exploiting these relationships, we aim to develop a more robust and informative model of coherence that can accurately distinguish between coherent and incoherent text. Our proposed model draws on recent advances in NLP, particularly those related to syntactic parsing and dependency relations [3]. We employ state-of-the-art syntactic parsing techniques to derive a dependency representation of the text, which we then utilize to identify patterns of syntactic structure that are indicative of coherence. Through a supervised learning approach, we train our model on a large dataset of annotated text and evaluate its performance using a series of benchmarks, including a classification task on news articles and a regression task on manual annotations of intentional structure for academic conference articles. Our results demonstrate that our method achieves high accuracy in distinguishing coherent from incoherent text, outperforming existing methods by a significant margin. Furthermore, we show that our syntactic patterns are correlated with human annotations of intentional structure, indicating the potential of our model for predicting the coherence of specific sections of text, such as abstracts and introductions. These findings have important implications for the development of more sophisticated NLP applications, which require a deeper understanding of the underlying structure of text.

Simple Task-Specific Bilingual Word Embeddings   Leveraging the vast amount of multilingual text data has become a crucial aspect of building effective natural language processing (NLP) models that can generalize across languages. One significant challenge in building such models is learning bilingual representations that capture the nuanced relationships between words in different languages. Traditional bilingual word embedding methods often require large parallel corpora, making them impractical for many applications. Furthermore, the performance of these methods is heavily dependent on the choice of embedding algorithm and the quality of the parallel data used for training. Recent advances in word embedding algorithms have led to the development of highly effective methods for learning monolingual word representations. However, when it comes to bilingual word embeddings, these methods often struggle to generalize across languages due to the lack of explicit supervision and the inherent complexity of bilingual relationships. In particular, conventional bilingual word embeddings often ignore the nuances of task-specific semantic relationships and instead focus on the co-occurrence of words across a general corpus. This can lead to representations that are not tailored to specific tasks and may not generalize well to unseen data. In light of these limitations, we propose a simple yet effective method for learning task-specific bilingual word embeddings. Our approach leverages off-the-shelf word embedding algorithms, which have been shown to be highly effective for monolingual word representation learning, to learn bilingual representations that are tailored to specific tasks. We accomplish this by employing a small dictionary of task-specific word equivalence classes, which we use to create mixed context-target pairs for training the off-the-shelf embedding models. This wrapper method has three key advantages: it is independent of the choice of embedding algorithm, it does not require parallel data, and it can be easily adapted to specific tasks by re-defining the equivalence classes. Our proposed method has the potential to overcome the limitations of conventional bilingual word embedding methods and provide a more flexible and effective approach to bilingual word representation learning. In this paper, we demonstrate the efficacy of our method on two prominent NLP tasks: unsupervised cross-language part-of-speech (POS) tagging and semi-supervised cross-language super sense (SuS) tagging. We compare our results to those obtained using off-the-shelf bilingual word embeddings and show that our method outperforms these baselines, highlighting the potential benefits of task-specific bilingual word embeddings for various NLP applications.

Relaxed Marginal Inference and its Application to Dependency Parsing The rise of probabilistic graphical models in Natural Language Processing (NLP) has revolutionized the field, enabling the development of sophisticated models for various tasks, including Dependency Parsing. However, as the complexity of these models increases, so does the computational cost of inference, making it a major bottleneck in many applications. One popular approach to addressing this issue has been relaxation methods, which aim to approximate the true marginal distributions of the model by relaxing the constraints of the original problem. These methods have seen significant success in Maximum a Posteriori (MAP) inference, enabling faster and more efficient inference on large-scale models. However, their application to marginal inference remains under-explored. Marginal inference is a crucial component in many NLP tasks, including conditional likelihood training, posterior decoding, and confidence estimation. While it provides a richer representation of the model's uncertainty, it is computationally more expensive than MAP inference, particularly for large models. This is because marginal inference requires computing the marginal distribution over all variables in the model, which can be tantamount to solving the original inference problem. In the context of graph-based models, this involves traversing the full factor graph, resulting in a computational cost that scales quadratically with the size of the graph. To mitigate this issue, we propose a novel approach for relaxed marginal inference, which leverages the strengths of relaxation methods while providing a more efficient solution to the marginal inference problem. Our approach extends the relaxation framework to the case of marginal inference, enabling the computation of marginal probabilities with reduced computational cost. We demonstrate the efficacy of our approach through a case study on second-order Dependency Parsing, a task that has garnered significant attention in NLP due to its importance in understanding sentence structure and meaning. By performing inference over a small subset of the full factor graph, we achieve a tenfold increase in parsing speed, with no loss in accuracy. Moreover, we derive a bound on the error of the marginal probabilities by a sub-graph with respect to the full graph, providing a theoretical justification for our approach. While this paper focuses on the use of Belief Propagation (BP) as the marginal inference method, our approach is general enough to be applied with any marginal inference method in the inner loop. This versatility makes our contribution valuable beyond the specific task of Dependency Parsing, with potential applications in several other NLP tasks that rely on marginal inference.

Introduction Topic modeling and word embedding are two prominent techniques used extensively in natural language processing tasks to derive latent semantics from large volumes of text data. Topic models, which emerged as a way to extract meaningful topics from text corpora, typically operate at a coarse granularity by modeling word co-occurrence patterns at the document or sentence level [1]. These models capture global relationships between words and are often useful for applications that require identifying abstract concepts or themes within texts. On the other hand, word embedding models work at a finer level of granularity, focusing on short-term dependencies between words within small sliding windows. By representing words as dense vectors, word embeddings succeed in capturing the rich semantic nuances of language, particularly for downstream tasks that require contextual understanding such as language translation and sentiment analysis [2]. Despite the success of these two techniques, they tend to operate with predefined assumptions about the desired level of granularity and typically fail to capture semantic relationships at multiple scales. For instance, topic models might overlook critical fine-grained semantic relationships between words, while word embeddings often lose sight of the global document-level context that may be crucial for more abstract, high-level tasks. Inspired by the individual strengths of topic modeling and word embedding, this work addresses a fundamental limitation in natural language processing by introducing a novel model named Latent Topic Embedding (LTE), designed to seamlessly integrate topic generation and embedding learning into a unified framework. With LTE, we pursue the ambitious goal of capturing word co-occurrence information at different levels of granularity – spanning coarse document-level topics to finer-grained semantic nuances – by retaining the best features of both techniques. Specifically, LTE is able to leverage the strengths of topic modeling in extracting high-level themes and concepts from large texts while incorporating the fine-grained understanding of word relationships provided by word embeddings. Furthermore, we develop an efficient Monte Carlo EM algorithm to effectively estimate the parameters of LTE. Our ultimate aim is to demonstrate the effectiveness and robustness of LTE in diverse natural language processing tasks that heavily rely on deep semantic understanding, thus engendering better performance than extant state-of-the-art methodologies in applications where high-precision and context-awareness are of paramount importance. This research endeavors to provide crucial insights into designing more holistic models that may automate the identification and interpretation of latent semantic relationships in large-scale texts, offered through more accurately and meaningfully capturing word co-occurrence information across multiple levels of granularity.

Automatic Corpus Expansion for Chinese Word Segmentation by Exploiting the Redundancy of Web Information Chinese word segmentation (CWS) is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP) for Chinese text processing, which plays a crucial role in many downstream applications, including sentiment analysis, information extraction, and machine translation. CWS aims to group a sequence of Chinese characters into words, which is a challenging task due to the nature of the Chinese language, where a single character can be part of multiple words and there is no delimiter to indicate word boundaries. Supervised learning methods have achieved remarkable success in CWS by employing large-scale annotated corpora, which provide sufficient labeled data to train high-performance models. However, one significant limitation of these supervised methods lies in their reliance on large-scale annotated corpora, which are often domain-specific and may not generalizable to new unseen domains without sufficient annotated data. Consequently, when encountering out-of-domain texts or newly emerging domains, the existing annotated corpora may not be sufficient to cover all possible linguistic patterns and word variants, which lead to a significant decline in the performance of traditional supervised CWS methods. Moreover, the process of creating and annotating relevant corpora is time-consuming, labor-intensive, and often requires extensive expertise, which poses a significant barrier to certain applications or domains where resources are scarce. In view of these challenges, it is crucial to explore novel methods that enable the expansion of existing annotated corpora, particularly for out-of-domain texts, to alleviate the dependence on large-scale and domain-specific annotated data. Towards this goal, this paper proposes an innovative approach to automatically expand the training corpus for CWS by exploiting the richness of web-sourced redundant information. The core hypothesis underlying our method is that a vast amount of easily and accurately segmented web data can be harnessed to effectively augment the existing annotation resources. By strategically leveraging the low-hanging fruits of available web information, we can fortify the existing corpus with an ample supply of relevant and reliably segmented text instances, thus engendering better performance for the original out-of-domain CWS task. The proposed method necessitates a two-stage approach. In the first stage, we enrich our native corpus by utilizing free and easily segmented web data. In the second stage, we leverage the preprocessed corpus to retrain more proficient and adaptable CWS models to better handle the initially complex segmentations that remain challenging.

Introduction Chinese Word Segmentation (CWS) and new word detection are two fundamental tasks in Natural Language Processing (NLP), with significant applications in various areas, such as text information retrieval, text summarization, and machine translation. Despite the rapid growth of digital content in the Chinese language, existing CWS models often suffer from slow training speeds, primarily due to the enormous size of datasets and the computational cost of processing high-dimensional features. Traditional off-line training methods, although providing good convergence speeds, are hardly sufficient in adapting to the rapidly evolving nature of Chinese text data, which entails frequent updates and incremental learning to accommodate new vocabulary, idioms, and linguistic expressions. The introduction of new words to the language is a common phenomenon, which poses significant challenges to word segmentation and downstream applications. When encountering unknown words, a word segmentation system may default to predefined strategies, such as ignoring, deleting, or inserting, that inevitably lead to decreased accuracy. A coarser solution would be to employ out-of-vocabulary (OOV) handling mechanisms, yet this might neglect the important inferences and relationships exhibited by the context in which the word appears. To fully address these challenges, building an accurate and robust integrated model for both word segmentation and new word detection is indispensable. In this paper, we design a novel joint model that aims to handle word segmentation and new word detection problems simultaneously, leveraging high-dimensional new features that include word-based features and enriched edge features (previously, label-transition features). Our high-dimensional feature set captures sophisticated inter-word relationships and local contextual patterns, significantly boosting the model's ability to tackle both tasks effectively. However, incorporating these features in the training process results in slower training times, making it difficult to efficiently update the model in response to new linguistic expressions, societal trending and volatile topics. Given this constraint, in this paper, we present a revolutionary solution to accelerate online training of the joint model even when dealing with large-scale datasets and complex feature sets. The fast online training method proposed in this paper is a sophisticated optimization technique that leverages frequency information for adaptive online gradient descent. The proposed method significantly boosts the training efficiency by more than an order of magnitude while maintaining comparable or even superior model accuracy rates. One of the most critical advantages of this method is its ability to be used extensively across various projects and application areas beyond the specific joint word segmentation and new word detection task introduced here.
