The Rating Game: Sentiment Rating Reproducibility from Text Introduction Sentiment analysis, a cornerstone of natural language processing (NLP), has gained significant attention in recent years due to its ubiquitous applications in consumer feedback analysis, product recommendations, opinion mining, and emotion detection. A crucial aspect of sentiment analysis lies in the use of labels, primarily in the form of ratings, which aim to encapsulate the sentiment expressed within review text. Ratings not only serve as a quality metric but also enable the development and evaluation of various sentiment analysis models. However, the premise underlying these rating-based models is often taken for granted: that ratings inherently reflect the sentiment of the corresponding text. While there is an abundance of research studying model-based sentiment analysis, the rating game, which involves human interpretation of sentiment from text, has received relatively less attention. The standard assumption is that human readers can accurately infer the sentiment ratings provided by authors, and that these ratings can be effectively used as labels for sentiment analysis models. However, a question arises: can humans truly infer sentiment ratings from text in a reliable and accurate manner? This paper seeks to address this gap in understanding by investigating the reproducibility of sentiment ratings from text. This study focuses on three primary goals: (i) assessing the ability of human readers to infer sentiment ratings from review text, (ii) comparing human performance with that of a regression model, and (iii) examining the impact of rating sources (i.e., original authors versus annotators) on the performance of sentiment analysis models. To achieve these objectives, we have curated a comprehensive dataset consisting of IMDb movie reviews with corresponding author-provided ratings. Additionally, these reviews have been re-annotated by both crowdsourced and trained annotators, allowing for a thorough evaluation of human reproducibility across different population groups. An understanding of how accurately humans can reproduce sentiment ratings is particularly important, as the widespread adoption of human-generated ratings as model labels may be impacted. Furthermore, exploring the relatively uncharted territory of annotator variability will engender a deeper comprehension of the complexities involved in assigning sentiment ratings. By quantitatively analyzing the reproducibility of ratings from author and annotators, we aim to contribute to the ongoing discussion on the reliability of human-generated labels and their suitability for use in sentiment analysis models. Our study casts a critical eye on the universal reliance on human ratings in sentiment analysis and endeavors to better grasp the relationships between the distribution of sentiment ratings assigned by humans and those assigned by sentiment analysis models.

Unsupervised Ranking Model for Entity Coreference Resolution Entity coreference resolution is a fundamental subtask in natural language processing that has garnered significant attention in recent years. Its importance stems from its role as a crucial step in deep language understanding, enabling efficient comprehension and accurate interpretation of text. In this context, coreference resolution refers to the process of identifying and linking expressions within a sentence or a text passage that refer to the same real-world entity. This complex task involves sophisticated reasoning and linguistic understanding, making it a challenging problem in the NLP community. Traditional approaches to coreference resolution have focused on supervised learning methods, relying heavily on manually annotated datasets to train and validate models. However, these approaches suffer from several limitations, including the need for extensive human labeling and the potential for biased results due to the variability of annotation schemes. Furthermore, supervised models often struggle with out-of-domain generalizability and the lack of robustness in handling entities with limited or no training data. Consequently, there is a pressing need for unsupervised models that can effectively resolve coreference without relying on extensive annotation or costly human labeling. In light of these challenges, we propose a novel, unsupervised ranking model for entity coreference resolution, which introduces a resolution mode variable to capture the nuanced relationships between entities. By adopting a generative approach, our model is able to infer coreference links without relying on explicit supervision. Instead, we utilize a ranking-based objective function to optimize the coreference scoring, allowing our model to automatically assign weights to different coreference solutions. This flexible framework enables our model to adapt to different coreference patterns, such as anaphora and cataphora, as well as to capture the relationships between entities across different discourse structures. Our proposed unsupervised model offers several advantages over traditional supervised approaches. Firstly, it obviates the need for extensive annotation and human labeling, reducing the costs associated with dataset creation and model training. Secondly, it exhibits improved out-of-domain generalizability, as it is not constrained by the limitations of annotated data. Lastly, it demonstrates enhanced robustness in handling entities with limited or no training data, making it a promising solution for many real-world NLP applications. In this paper, we present a comprehensive evaluation of our proposed unsupervised ranking model on the English data from the CoNLL-2012 shared task. Our results show that our model achieves a competitive 58.44% F1 score on the CoNLL metric, outperforming the Stanford deterministic system (Lee et al., 2013) by 3.01%.

Introduction The ability of a machine to refer to objects within a visual context has been a long-standing goal in artificial intelligence and computer vision research. Specifically, referring expression generation (REG) has been a topic of significant interest, aiming to develop systems that can produce accurate and descriptive labels for objects in images, such as "the red car" or "the person wearing a hat." Most existing REG research focuses on the 'one-shot reference' approach, where the system attempts to generate a single, discriminative expression that accurately describes the target object. However, this approach may not be optimal in real-world scenarios, particularly when the system's understanding of the object's attributes and categories is uncertain. In contrast, human reference establishment often follows a more iterative approach, known as 'installments,' where referring information is gradually provided until an accurate identification is confirmed. For instance, in a conversation, a companion might point to an object and say "it's the colorful one" and then, upon the listener's request for further clarification, say "the one with the big wheels." This sequential and interactive process can significantly improve the accuracy of object reference, even with uncertain access to object attributes and categories. Inspired by this observation, we investigate whether incorporating 'installments' into a technical REG system can facilitate more accurate and effective object reference. Specifically, we focus on generating referring expressions for objects in photographs, a challenging task due to the variety of visual features, expressions, and contextual dependencies involved. Our approach relies on the integration of a recently introduced model of grounded word meaning with a context-aware, referential 'installments' strategy. By splitting the generation process into multiple steps, our system can adjust and refine its output based on the user's feedback and the available context, increasing the likelihood of accurate object reference. In this work, we present an in-depth evaluation of our proposed REG system, assessing its performance on a large dataset of referring expressions for objects in images. Our experiments reveal that the incremental nature of the 'installments' approach can indeed enhance the referential success of the system, even when faced with uncertain access to object attributes and categories. Furthermore, our results demonstrate the system's ability to adapt and learn from user feedback, refining its object reference over time. By shedding light on the benefits of 'installments' in REG, our research contributes to the advancement of human-computer interaction and visual reference establishment, ultimately improving the ability of machines to accurately and effectively communicate with users.

Mine new business opportunities: Identifying Trend related Products by Leveraging Commercial Intents from Microblogs Introduction The advent of social media and online platforms has revolutionized the way individuals consume and interact with information, significantly influencing consumer behavior and product choices. E-commerce companies, in particular, have long recognized the importance of staying ahead of emerging trends to capitalize on new business opportunities. However, rapidly identifying related products that capitalize on these trends has proven to be a significant challenge for businesses. Trends such as "Air Pollution," "Sustainable Living," or "Health and Wellness" can create significant market opportunities, with products like face masks, reusable straws, or probiotic supplements experiencing exponential growth as a result. Identifying these trend-related products is a complex task that requires depth and breadth of knowledge in various domains. First, an individual or organization must stay informed about current trends and their dynamics to have the potential to benefit from them. Second, they must be adept at understanding consumer behavior associated with these trends. For instance, knowing how social norms influence individuals' attitudes toward product categories related to a particular trend can contribute to informed business decision making. Finally, businesses need the capacity to rapidly translate these insights into targeted actions, such as developing new products, modifying existing ones or improving their marketing. In this paper, we focus on addressing the very first challenge: rapidly identifying related products for trends that have the potential to yield new business opportunities. Commercial intentions captured from social media, such as microblogs, can provide valuable insights into emerging trends. However, such insights must be systematically collected and processed to provide actionable intelligence for businesses. To this end, we emphasize the importance of identifying the underlying structure of commercial intents by analyzing relevant indicia from microblogs that reflect the specific context of a trend. Tackling this task requires advanced methodologies that leverage the sheer volume and breadth of consumer-generated information. This encompasses natural language processing techniques for extracting commercial information from microblog posts, coupled with network-based approaches for capturing the latent relationships between various product categories that may be associated with a particular trend. Towards this end, we develop a graph-based framework for modeling and ranking trend-related products. This study integrates various pieces of knowledge, including leveraging well-established techniques in NLP, graph learning, as well as advanced statistical methods to enable prediction of related products. We further demonstrate this approach through thorough experiments with evaluations of various performance metrics and demonstrate the potential applications and improvements in the markets of various e-commerce companies through evaluations of our proposed model compared to other baseline approaches.

Automatic Adaptation of Annotation Standards: Chinese Word Segmentation and POS Tagging - A Case Study Human-annotated corpora are invaluable resources in natural language processing and machine learning tasks such as sequence labeling, text classification, and parsing. However, these valuable resources are scarce and often require significant human effort and expense to create. In an effort to maximize the efficiency and effectiveness of these resources, researchers and practitioners seek to reuse and adapt existing corpora to new annotation standards. One glaring obstacle in this endeavor is the prevalence of multiple, incompatible annotated corpora, where different annotation guidelines or standards are utilized. Given the significant cost and resources required for human-annotated data collection, this inconsistency appears to amount to an unfortunate waste of valuable human effort. This scenario is particularly pertinent in the realm of treebanking and sequence labeling, where annotation guidelines standardization can critically influence the generalizability and reproducibility of empirical results and findings in the field. Moreover, the lack of established standards and guidelines can hamper cross-project comparisons and more effectively advance our understanding of the underlying linguistic and cognitive mechanisms. Our goal in this research, therefore, is to address this pressing issue by investigating and developing an automated adaptation strategy that enables knowledge transfer between corpora with different annotation standards. We study a particularly challenging and understudied domain, Chinese word segmentation and part-of-speech tagging, where currently, there exist multiple corpora with different and incompatible annotation guidelines or standards. Chinese, as a language with no morphology, poses a unique set of challenges to part-of-speech (POS) tagging and word segmentation tasks. With its complex character repertoires and rich pragmatic contexts, Chinese accents a delicate balance between semantic and syntactic factors. Given these significant linguistic challenges, current automated annotation methods demonstrate limited precision and effectiveness when applied to the segmentation and tagging of Chinese text. In light of this critical need for more accurate and efficient annotation methods, our proposed strategy leverages knowledge transfer and adaptation techniques to aid in the automatic adaptation of annotation standards. By leveraging an existing annotated corpus, such as the large and lexically diverse People's Daily corpus, we adapt annotations for a differently annotated corpus like the smaller, but more popular, Penn Chinese Treebank. We investigate the efficacy of this method within the challenging context of Chinese word segmentation and POS tagging. Experimental results demonstrate this automated adaptation strategy delivers significant improvements in both Chinese word segmentation and POS tagging accuracies.

Introduction The exponential growth of online content has led to a pressing need for effective methods to automatically extract structured knowledge from unstructured natural language text. Open Information Extraction (OIE) has emerged as a promising approach to address this challenge, as it enables the identification of surface relations and their arguments from text in an unsupervised and domain-independent manner. Unlike traditional relation extraction methods that rely on annotated corpora or manual rules, OIE systems aim to extract facts without requiring a priori knowledge of the domain or the specific entities involved. However, OIE has also been criticized for producing lengthy and imprecise extractions that often contain unnecessary information, making them difficult to interpret and reuse. In an effort to overcome these limitations, numerous OIE systems have been proposed, which employ various techniques to improve the precision, recall, and readability of extracted facts. These methods range from simple filtering approaches that remove stop words or overly specific terms to more sophisticated techniques that incorporate machine learning models, semantic grids, or ontologies. While these efforts have led to significant improvements, a major challenge remains in balancing the precision and recall of extracted facts, as overly permissive systems often sacrifice one for the other. To address this challenge, we propose MinIE, a novel OIE system that aims to provide compact, semantically enriched extractions with high precision and recall. The core insights behind MinIE are two-fold. Firstly, we argue that certain types of information, such as polarity, modality, attribution, and quantities, are often expressed in a way that distracts from the main relation or argument being described. To mitigate this effect, MinIE encodes these semantic annotations in the extraction process but omits them from the final output, allowing users to easily identify and explore these nuances without cluttering the main extraction. Secondly, MinIE introduces a novel pruning mechanism that identifies and removes parts of the extraction that are deemed overly specific or redundant, resulting in condensed but still informative and accurate extractions. MinIE thus represents a critical step towards addressing the longstanding trade-off between precision and recall in OIE, as well as the emerging challenge of producing informative but digestible extractions that resonate with various user communities. By incorporating these key insights, we aim to demonstrate that MinIE can achieve state-of-the-art performance on a range of real-world datasets while producing shorter, semantically enriched extractions. Our experimental evaluation will demonstrate the effectiveness of MinIE in the context of OIE, evaluating its performance against a range of competitive systems and illuminating its key strengths and limitations.

Exploiting Web-Derived Selectional Preference to Improve Statistical Dependency Parsing Dependency parsing is a fundamental task in natural language processing (NLP), aiming at identifying the grammatical structure of a sentence by modeling the relationships between words, such as subject-verb and verb-object. Despite the significant advances in recent years, especially with the emergence of deep learning-based approaches, statistical dependency parsing remains challenging, particularly for long and complex sentences. This is partly due to the sophisticated linguistic structures and idiomatic expressions used in natural languages, which often cannot be captured by simple statistical models. Traditional statistical dependency parsing methods typically rely on manually designed grammars and annotated corpora to learn the linguistic rules governing word dependencies. However, these approaches are often limited by their reliance on the quality and quantity of training data, which may not be readily available for many languages. Moreover, as the complexity of language structures increases, the accuracy of these models tends to degrade due to the coarseness of their representation. The selectional preference (SP) theory has been proposed to address this issue by modeling the lexical-semantic compatibility between words, such as which noun can be selected as the subject by a verb. Early works on SP have primarily focused on learning word-to-class relations using linguistic resources like WordNet and annotated corpora. For example, some models represent the SP of a word as a binary vector mapping each class to a scalar value indicating the likelihood of the word being associated with that class. This approach has led to improvements in various NLP tasks, such as part-of-speech (POS) tagging and sentiment analysis. However, the limitation of these SP methods lies in their applicability to high-level linguistic phenomena, where word dependencies are characterized by complex patterns that cannot be fully captured by a simple word-to-class relationship. Furthermore, the lack of adequate training data for certain languages and task domains has obstructed the widespread adoption of these SP-based models. Recent advances in web-scale data collection and processing have made it possible to tap into the vast amounts of unsupervised data available on the internet. By leveraging web-derived selectional preferences, we can extend the applicability of SP-based methods to more complex linguistic structures and tasks. In this paper, we propose a novel approach that incorporates web-derived selectional preferences to improve statistical dependency parsing. Our method explores a new dimension of word dependencies, namely the word-to-word selectional preferences, by utilizing web-scale data.

Joint Annotation of Search Queries Introduction ------------ The exponential growth of the web has led to a commensurate surge in search engine queries, revolutionizing the way we seek and consume information. As a result, accurately processing and understanding search queries has become a critical component of modern information retrieval systems. Marking up search queries with linguistic annotations such as part-of-speech tags, capitalization, and segmentation is an essential step towards unlocking their meaning and improving the effectiveness of retrieval algorithms. However, search queries pose a unique set of challenges to existing natural language processing (NLP) tools, due to their idiosyncratic nature and brevity. Traditional NLP techniques are often designed to process longer natural language texts, such as documents, articles and books, which are inherently more informative and coherent than search queries. In contrast, search queries are typically short, comprising a few words or even just a single keyword, and are frequently composed of fragmented phrases or colloquialisms. These characteristics make it difficult for existing NLP tools to accurately annotate search queries, which not only hampers the effectiveness of information retrieval, but also raises concerns about user experience and satisfaction. Current approaches to annotating search queries heavily rely on rule-based methods, pre-defined dictionaries and controlled vocabularies to infer the intent of the query. These methods, while somewhat effective for specific domains and applications, suffer from several limitations. Firstly, they require considerable manual effort and domain expertise to define and populate the annotation rules and dictionaries. Secondly, they quickly become outdated as the search space and User behaviour evolve over time. Thirdly, they often fail to capture the nuances and complexities of natural language usage, leading to inadequate annotations and sub-optimal query processing outcomes. Against this backdrop, there is a pressing need for more flexible and adaptive approaches to annotating search queries. This calls for robust machine learning methods that can learn to annotate search queries from limited labeled data and make accurate predictions even when faced with unfamiliar or ambiguous queries. The task is indeed daunting, as it demands not only accurate annotation of each individual term within the query, but also consideration of the context, intent and intent ambivalence of the user behind the query. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to annotating search queries using a probabilistic model that jointly annotates all aspects of the query, including the independent annotations and their inter-relationships. Building on this model, we explore the possibility of incremental learning and evaluating on multiple annotation tasks with high accuracy.

Query Weighting for Ranking Model Adaptation Ranking models have become an essential component in various information retrieval tasks such as Web search, product recommendation, and information retrieval over large document collections. However, real-world applications often require adapting ranking models across multiple domains, which is a challenging problem known as ranking model adaptation. Ranking model adaptation involves transferring the knowledge learned in a source domain to a target domain with limited or no relevant data. While significant research has been dedicated to ranking model adaptation, it still remains an open issue in the field of information retrieval and natural language processing. A major bottleneck in ranking model adaptation is the proper handling of data from different domains, particularly the varying query distributions. Typical approaches to ranking model adaptation rely heavily on document weighting, where the importance of each document is estimated separately and combined with the relevance scores provided by the ranking models to obtain the final ranking order. However, this approach often suffers from the "Queries are not alone" problem. In real-world applications, a single query may have thousands, if not tens of thousands, of relevant documents. The ranking task is, therefore, divided among multiple instances, making it reasonable to perform importance weighting at the query level instead of the document level. Query weighting for ranking model adaptation is the process of assigning different weights to different queries based on certain criteria, which is often not well-studied. We argue that query weighting can potentially alleviate the "queries are not alone" problem by treating each query as an independent unit that captures its internal semantic properties and interdependence with document instances. This means that the assignment of weights to different queries could be optimized such that the ranking performance on the target domain can be improved. Query weighting is also related to the field of domain adaptation that considers the gap between source and target domains and adjusts the representation space accordingly. Since the source and target domains may have different query distributions, simply applying the document-level weighting methods from the source domain can result in a sub-optimal adaptation performance. Query weighting can help address this issue by recognizing that the same query could be asked in multiple domains and assigning more importance to the target queries that are more informative or have a higher expected accuracy. By adaptively adjusting the query weights, we can potentially improve the adaptability of the ranking models and achieve better ranking performance in the target domain.

Introduction Opinion mining and sentiment analysis have become increasingly important areas of research in natural language processing, as they have the potential to automatically extract useful information from large amounts of text data, such as customer reviews, product descriptions, and social media posts. One critical challenge in opinion mining is to identify opinion entities and relations, which are essential for understanding the context in which an opinion is expressed and the related entities or target objects. Opinion entities refer to the words or phrases that a customer's opinion is about, such as a product name, a brand, or a service. Opinion relations, on the other hand, specify the type of opinion relationship between the opinion entity and the entity being talked about, such as "from" (e.g., "customers are the source of this product") or "about" (e.g., "this product is about ease of use"). Semantic Relation Classification via Hierarchical Recurrent Neural Network with Attention The rise of natural language processing (NLP) has brought about an increasing interest in automatic semantic relation classification – extracting information about the relationships between entities and concepts from raw text data. A fundamental problem in NLP research, semantic relation classification has far-reaching applications in various tasks such as question answering, sentiment analysis, and information retrieval. However, accurately classifying semantic relations has proven challenging due to the complexity and potential ambiguity of natural language, often leading to suboptimal performance when using traditional machine learning approaches. In recent years, deep learning models have shown remarkable improvement over traditional methods in various NLP tasks, including semantic relation classification. Among these, recurrent neural networks (RNNs) stand out as a primary choice due to their ability to learn sequential representations of input data, which is invaluable for modeling the order-dependent, sequential structure typically found in natural language. However, in the context of semantic relation classification, RNNs can be constrained by their tendency to treat all input elements equally, neglecting important context information and hindering the model's ability to attentively select the most pertinent pieces of information for relation classification. To address this challenge, several researchers have proposed incorporating various adaptations into the traditional RNN architecture, such as incorporating pre-trained language embeddings, cascading feed-forward neural networks on top of the RNN layers, or combining the strengths of different models with encouraging results. Nevertheless, most of these adaptations rely heavily on additional hand-crafted features or assume pre-labeled datasets that are although successful have found to be restrictive in scenarios where the amount and quality of labeled data are in significantly short supply. Therefore, there is a pressing need for a supervised modeling method that is not only able to effectively and efficiently represent and analyze sequential data, but also does so while not requiring large amounts of task-specific annotated data to pre-train the network before using it on new relation classification tasks. Given the lack of hand-crafted knowledge in the model, a sophisticated unsupervised data preparation scheme is urgently required. One compelling solution that has been proposed is the use of context subsequences within the raw sentence. This has been supported through research which shows that diving the sentence into these subsequences enables the neural network to encode context of local sub-sentences separately to course the important relations present in local-area quickest.

Reinforcement Learning of Cooperative Persuasive Dialogue Policies using Framing Introduction: Persuasive dialogue is a fundamental aspect of human daily life, influencing various decisions and actions that impact individuals and societies alike. In contrast, current state-of-the-art conversational systems often fail to adapt to the nuances of human-like persuasive dialogue, resulting in unnatural interactions that may deter users from taking desired actions. Recently, reinforcement learning (RL) has emerged as a promising paradigm for learning efficient policies in conversational dialogue systems. This approach has shown impressive results in various applications, such as task-oriented dialogue systems and game-playing agents. However, traditional RL methods often overlook the fundamental characteristics of human persuasiveness, notably the use of manipulative and emotive language known as framing, which is inherently more difficult to incorporate into reinforcement learning frameworks. To close this gap, this paper proposes a novel approach to learning cooperative persuasive dialogue policies using framing through RL. A key element of our approach is the design of user simulators and reward functions tailored specifically to the dynamic and often cryptic nature of persuasive dialogue. By leveraging RL, we enable conversational systems to automatically learn the complex dependencies between dialogue acts and linguistic choices relevant to persuasive tasks, thereby improving their capacity to persuade users effectively. Our work is grounded in the understanding that certain linguistic patterns, including framing, have been found to significantly influence persuasion. Yet, developing dialogue systems that leverage framing effectively remains a challenge due to the difficulty in defining optimal dialogue policies that balance the goals of persuasion while accounting for the complexities of human decision-making processes. User simulators provide a means to incorporate the complexity of human decision-making without incurring the high costs associated with employing real users. However, designing these simulators requires significant expertise in conversational systems, linguistics and human decision-making processes. To address these challenges, we first present a comprehensive framework for constructing user simulators that accurately capture the characteristics of human persuasiveness. Building on this foundation, we develop a reward function that quantifies the persuasiveness of dialogue policies. The reward function employs metrics such as user response rates and persuasion success rates to evaluate the effectiveness of dialogue policies. This enables RL algorithms to optimize the policy parameters to maximize user persuasion. Through a series of experiments, we evaluate the performance of our proposed RL framework using both user simulators and real users.

Corroborating Text Evaluation Results with Heterogeneous Measures The rise of automatic text production, such as machine translation and summarization, has revolutionized the way we process and consume information. As these technologies continue to advance, there is a growing need for accurate evaluation methods that can assess their quality and effectiveness. Traditionally, text evaluation results have primarily relied on n-gram based measures, such as BLEU and ROUGE, which quantify the similarity between machine-generated and human-produced text. However, with the proliferation of sophisticated measures proposed in recent years, the question arises as to why these newer approaches remain largely neglected in practical applications. On the surface, the reasons for this disparity may seem obvious. More complex evaluation measures often require significantly more computational resources and technical expertise to implement and interpret. Furthermore, the additional insights provided by these measures may not always outweigh the added complexity and potential for conflicting results. Yet, despite these challenges, it is essential to revisit the state of the art in text evaluation and re-examine the justification for relying primarily on legacy metrics. One key factor in the dearth of adoption for more advanced measures lies in the lack of a clear understanding of their properties and how they relate to the fundamental goals of evaluation. Evaluating the quality of automatically produced text involves assessing how closely it aligns with human-generated references. While measures like BLEU and ROUGE excel in this regard, their critique is limited to specific aspects of similarity. In contrast, more sophisticated measures may capture nuances such as contextual understanding, semantic coherence, or even the stylistic aptitude of machine-generated text. To bridge this gap, in this paper we undertake an in-depth analysis of the state of the art in text evaluation measures. We aim to illuminate the underlying rationale behind the existing toolkit and pinpoint key attributes that are inherent to evaluation metrics based on similarity to human-produced references. Our empirical investigation demonstrates that these metrics uniformly satisfy a set of properties that are pivotal to reliable and accurate evaluation. These findings have far-reaching implications for the adoption of heterogeneous measures to corroborate text evaluation results. By combining multiple metrics with different strengths and weaknesses, we can raise the overall reliability of the evaluation process and enhance confidence in our conclusions. Furthermore, we show that the combined reliability of measures is directly proportional to their diversity, providing a quantitative means to select the optimal set of metrics for any given task.

Introduction Answering natural language questions that require multiple steps of reasoning is a longstanding challenge in artificial intelligence, with far-reaching implications for applications such as question answering, retrieval and dialogue systems. To address this challenge, significant advances have been made in the development of various neural models that are capable of interpreting and processing human language in a way that is both computationally efficient and cognitively plausible [1][2]. However, despite these advances, many of these models remain shallow and sequential in nature, lacking the deeper understanding of compositional meaning that is necessary to tackle the complexity of natural language questions. In this paper, we take a novel approach to addressing this challenge by introducing a neural model of compositional denotational semantics (CDS) that is inspired by formal approaches to semantics [3]. Our goal is to develop an end-to-end differentiable model for interpreting questions about a knowledge graph (KG), which is able to capture the compositional structure of natural language and learn a grounding for the complete sentence that answers the question. We take as our starting point the idea that each span of text has both a denotation, which captures the grounded meaning of the text in the KG, and an ungrounded aspect, which captures the aspects of meaning that are not yet grounded in the KG. By recursively combining these constituent spans using learned composition modules, our model is able to capture the complex relationships between the elements of a sentence and build a rich understanding of the compositional meaning of the sentence. One of the key insights of our approach is that the ungrounded aspects of meaning can be represented as trainable vectors, which can be used to parameterize the composition functions that combine the constituent spans. This allows our model to capture a wide range of challenging semantic operators, including quantifiers, disjunctions and composed relations, and to learn both the composition operators and the output structure of the sentence jointly from the task supervision. Additionally, by building a parse chart that subsumes all possible parses of the sentence, our model is able to infer latent syntactic structure and to generalize well to longer questions than seen in its training data. Our approach has a number of connections to formal approaches to semantics, including Montague grammar [4] and categorial grammar [5]. However, unlike these approaches, which are typically non-differentiable and require manual annotation of the parse tree, our model is fully differentiable and learns both the composition operators and the output structure of the sentence automatically from task supervision.

Introduction Statistical Machine Translation (SMT) has witnessed a tremendous advancement from its early word-based paradigm to more sophisticated phrase/rule-based paradigms. This evolution has significantly enhanced the quality of machine translation systems by capturing more nuanced aspects of language, such as phrase structures and contextual dependencies. However, despite these improvements, SMT systems still largely overlook the importance of high-level semantic information, such as topics, in informing translation decisions. Previous work in topic modeling for SMT has primarily focused on incorporating topic information at the word level, using techniques like Latent Dirichlet Allocation (LDA) to represent source sentences as mixtures of topics, and translating words based on their topic affinities. While these approaches have shown promise, they still operate within the limitations of the word-based paradigm and often rely on crude approximations of phrase meanings. In this paper, we take a significant step forward by proposing a Topic Similarity Model (TSM) for Hierarchical Phrase-based Translation (HPBT). Our approach targets the synchronous rule level, which operates at the heart of HPBT, where the translation system dynamically generates translation rules to cover the source language. By associating each synchronous rule with a topic distribution, we create a rich representation of the rule's meaning, which can be leveraged to improve translation quality and efficiency. Specifically, our model leverages topic similarity between synchronous rules and given documents to select the most relevant rules for translation, effectively exploiting the high-level semantic information that topics provide. Our motivation for exploring topic similarity at the synchronous rule level is twofold. Firstly, by focusing on the rule level, we can capture the nuanced phrase structures and contextual dependencies that are crucial for accurate translation. Secondly, by incorporating topic information, we can provide a more principled and effective way of selecting translation rules, moving beyond the simplistic word-based approaches of the past. This combination of phrase-based translation and topic modeling is expected to yield a significant improvement in translation performance compared to existing methods that operate at the word level. We will demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach on the NIST Chinese-to-English translation task, one of the most challenging language pairs in SMT research. Our experimental results will show that TSM outperforms the baseline HPBT system and achieves better performance and faster speed compared to previous approaches that work at the word level. These findings not only confirm the merits of our proposed approach but also highlight the potential of topic similarity modeling in pushing the boundaries of SMT research.

Introduction Historical documents represent a crucial source of information for a wide range of disciplines, from linguistics and history to sociology and anthropology. However, these documents often present significant challenges to researchers and scholars due to their extant nature, written in languages that have undergone considerable evolution over time. Among the several factors that hinder the understanding of historical documents, orthographic variation stands out as a particularly pressing issue. Archaic spellings, obsolete shorthand symbols, and idiosyncratic notations are just a few of the manifestations of orthographic variation that can be found in historical texts. Orthographic variation in historical documents arises from the changing nature of language, the evolution of shorthand systems, and the modification of writing conventions over time. As a result, the depth and complexity of these documents can make them difficult to decipher without extensive knowledge of the field and the language of the era in which the documents were written. Furthermore, the abundance of orthographic variation in historical documents can give rise to inconsistencies in automatic transcription, which in turn can distort the accuracy of downstream analysis and applications such as named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, and text classification. Digital tool development, particularly in image and text analysis, has made significant strides in addressing various issues associated with historical documents. Optical character recognition (OCR) techniques and related technologies, for instance, have been instrumental in improving the efficiency and accuracy of document transcription. Current OCR tools employ a range of strategies to tackle orthographic variation, with the goal of producing so-called diplomatic transcriptions that preserve these variant spellings intact. This ensures the integrity and authenticity of historical documents, which are critical factors in gaining profound insights from them. However, there are scenarios where diplomats transcription does not constitute the final desired outcome. Many end tasks require transcriptions with standardized orthography, which enables tasks related to named entity recognition, sentiment analysis, information retrieval, and many more to reach the optimal results. Nonetheless, creating a model that balances the requirement of reproducing historical documents in the way they were written, while also creating transcriptions in standardized form, poses a considerable challenge in itself. In this context, we seek to address the ambivalence between diplomatic transcription and the requirement of producing well-formed orthography. We propose a joint transcription model, operated in an unsupervised mode, that fits well with both the requirement of handling the prevalent nature of historical documents, plus assure that transcriptions generated reflect a standard orthography - understandable in various machine applications.

Introduction The widespread use of geographic information systems (GIS) has become an essential aspect of our daily lives. One such system that has gained immense popularity is the OpenStreetMap (OSM) database, a collaborative project that provides up-to-date, free, editable maps of the world. With its vast and ever-growing repository of geographic data, OSM offers immense potential for research and development of novel applications that require access to geographic information. However, querying OSM is a complex task, especially for average users who lack experience with database queries or programming languages. The current interface of OSM requires users to either write SQL queries or manually select specific features, which can be a daunting task for non-experts. This creates a significant barrier for a broader audience to explore and utilize geographic data for various applications. Consequently, an essential step forward in enriching the experience of using OSM is the development of a natural language interface (NLI) that allows users to query the database using everyday language. This would enable users to directly access and utilize geographic data by simply submitting a short query, such as "Find restaurants near me" or "Show the north side of the city." Furthermore, an NLI for OSM should ideally support various languages, allowing it to be a global interface. To achieve this, the development of an NLI requires two key components: a dataset of annotated natural language queries and a parser that can accurately translate these queries into the corresponding database query operations. Recently, significant progress has been made in the development of semantic parsers that can accurately translate natural language queries into machine-readable formats. However, such parsers have mostly been trained using datasets that are limited to single languages or a few specific domains. Moreover, the generalization capabilities of these parsers are often restricted to narrow and pre-defined ontologies without allowing for lexical variability or syntactic complexity. To move towards the development of an accurate and efficient NLI for OSM, researchers require a large and diverse dataset of annotated natural language queries that can support the learning of a robust parser. This, in turn, demands the creation of a comprehensive corpus that can capture the diversity of queries that a multilingual natural language interface should support. It is within this context that this paper makes a significant contribution to the field. In this work, we release a novel corpus of natural language queries paired with machine-readable formulae that can be executed against the geographic data stored in the OSM database.

Extracting Spatial Entities and Relations in Korean Text Spatial information extraction has become increasingly important in recent years, with applications in various fields such as geographic information systems (GIS), natural language processing (NLP), and artificial intelligence (AI). One of the primary goals of spatial information extraction is to identify and represent spatial entities and their relationships, allowing users to retrieve and reason about spatial information effectively [1]. However, the extraction of spatial entities and relations in Korean text remains a challenging task due to the unique characteristics of the Korean language and the lack of language resources. Conventional spatial information extraction systems have primarily focused on English text, and several competitions, such as the SpaceEval challenge [2], have been organized to evaluate the performance of these systems. While some of the techniques developed for English text have shown promising results, they are not directly applicable to Korean text due to linguistic differences between the two languages. For instance, Korean is an agglutinative language that uses a unique grammar system, and its syntax and morphology have significant implications for the extraction of spatial entities and relations [3]. Furthermore, the lack of Korean language resources, including annotated datasets and pre-trained models, has hindered the development of effective spatial information extraction systems for Korean text. Researchers have attempted to adapt English-based techniques to Korean text by using machine translation, morphological analysis, and syntax-based approaches [4][5]. However, these methods may not be optimal for Korean text, as they may not accurately capture the nuances of the language. For instance, machine translation may lead to errors in translation, while morphological analysis may miss the complexities of Korean grammar. Moreover, syntax-based approaches may not be effective in identifying spatial relationships, as they rely heavily on the surface-level syntax of the sentence. In this paper, we propose a novel approach to extracting spatial entities and relations in Korean text. Our method consists of two main components: the first is a spatial entity extraction model that uses word vectors to alleviate over-generation and identify relevant spatial entities; the second is a spatial relation extraction model that leverages dependency parse labels to find proper arguments in relations. By utilizing these two models, we aim to accurately identify and represent spatial entities and their relationships in Korean text, enabling effective spatial information extraction. In our experiments, we evaluate the performance of our models on a dataset of Korean texts and demonstrate their effectiveness in extracting spatial entities and relations accurately and efficiently.

Learning Whom to Trust with MACE Introduction The proliferation of big data has generated a growing need for cost-effective and efficient methods for annotating and evaluating large datasets. Non-expert annotation services like Amazon's Mechanical Turk (AMT) have filled this gap, offering quick and affordable access to categorical annotations that can be used to train and evaluate machine learning systems. However, while AMT and other crowdsourcing platforms have facilitated the widespread adoption of data-intensive machine learning approaches, they also create a potential source of noise and bias in training data. Unfortunately, some human annotators may intentionally choose bad labels in order to maximize their pay, undermining the accuracy of the resulting models. Identifying and mitigating the effects of manipulative annotators is a challenging and important problem, as it can have significant consequences for the performance and reliability of downstream models. While some researchers have developed complex approaches to detect and correct errors in labeled data, these methods often require large amounts of labeled data, extensive computational resources, and sophisticated statistical knowledge. However, more often than not, these existing methods fall short in their ability to scale to the large, rapidly accumulating datasets that underlie many modern machine learning applications. To address these challenges, we propose a novel approach to identifying trustworthy annotators and predicting accurate labels in the face of potential manipulation. Our approach, which we call MACE (Multi-Annotator Competence Estimation), is based on a simple yet effective item-response theory (IRT) model that learns to identify trustworthy annotators and predict correct labels in an unsupervised fashion. We demonstrate that MACE achieves state-of-the-art performance in terms of both predicted label accuracy and trustworthiness estimates, outperforming standard baselines by a considerable margin. We also explore a variety of extensions and refinements to MACE, including the incorporation of prior knowledge and Variational Bayes inference to further improve its performance. In the remainder of this paper, we provide a detailed overview of our approach, including the technical foundations and computational implementation of MACE. We also present a comprehensive evaluation of MACE's performance on a range of benchmark datasets, comparing it favorably with state-of-the-art alternatives. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the broader machine learning community, highlighting the potential benefits of MACE for improving the accuracy and reliability of downstream models in data-intensive applications. By demonstrating the effectiveness of MACE in identifying trustworthy annotators and predicting accurate labels, we aim to make a significant contribution to the field of machine learning, and to establish a new standard for robust and reliable data annotation in the age of big data

Dialogue Generation Using Multi-turn Reasoning Neural Networks Introduction Human conversations are inherently multi-turn processes, often involving a series of back-and-forth exchanges between interlocutors. Effective dialogue generation models, therefore, must be capable of capturing the sequential nature of conversational interactions, incorporating contextual clues from previous turns to respond appropriately to queries. While significant progress has been made in developing neural dialogue generation models, the majority of these approaches focus on single-turn conversations, neglecting the potential of multi-turn reasoning mechanisms to generate more informative and engaging responses. Recent advancements in document comprehension have introduced multiturn reasoning processes, which involve multiple rounds of question-answering to derive accurate document representations. Inspired by these developments, this paper explores the application of multiturn reasoning neural networks to dialogue generation, adapting the concept of document comprehension to handle conversational sessions as "documents" and user queries as "questions." By representing conversation sessions as memories, our approach enables the incorporation of contextual clues from previous turns to extend and refine user queries. This results in more diverse and acceptable responses, as evidenced in our experimental results on Japanese 10-sentence (5-round) conversation modeling. To address the issue of speaker-specific topics and opinions, we propose a novel approach of separating the single memory used for document comprehension into different groups for speaker-specific topic and opinion embedding. Specifically, our model leverages the queries' memory, responses' memory, and their unified memory, following the time sequence of the conversation session. This allows our model to capture the dynamics of conversational interactions, generating responses that are not only contextually relevant but also attentive to the speakers' individual perspectives. The goal of this paper is to present a generalizable dialogue generation approach that incorporates the benefits of multi-turn reasoning, effectively responding to user queries and engaging in more informed and respectful conversations. By demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach on state-of-the-art single-turn and non-reasoning baselines, we aim to establish the significance of multi-turn reasoning neural networks in the field of dialogue generation, paving the way for more sophisticated and realistic conversational AI systems. The remainder of this paper is organized as follows: Section 2 presents a detailed description of our proposed approach, including the architecture of our multi-turn reasoning neural network and the methods used for speaker-specific topic and opinion embedding. Section 3 provides the experimental setup and results, demonstrating the effectiveness of our approach on a range of benchmark tasks.

A Generalisation of Lexical Functions for Composition in Distributional Semantics Introduction: The advent of distributional semantics has revolutionised the field of natural language processing, providing a paradigm that leverages the statistical properties of word co-occurrence to infer meaning representations of individual words. Over the past two decades, researchers have developed numerous algorithms that successfully capture the semantics of single words by representing them as points in a high-dimensional vector space. This approach has been instrumental in a wide range of applications, including word sense induction, sentiment analysis, and question answering. However, despite its success in capturing the meaning of individual words, the distributional semantics framework has fallen short in compositional tasks – i.e., tasks that involve combining words into larger units, such as phrases, sentences, or even paragraphs. Composition is a fundamental aspect of human language understanding. We regularly come across linguistic expressions that are formed by the combination of multiple words, and our ability to comprehend these expressions hinges on our ability to understand how the individual words contribute to the overall meaning. The distributional semantics framework has struggled to address composition, primarily due to its reliance on word-level representations. While the framework excels at capturing the nuances of individual word meanings, it is not well-equipped to model the interactions between multiple words. One approach to addressing composition is through the concept of lexical functions, which were first introduced by Mel'cuk (1982). Lexical functions describe the way in which a word can be combined with another word to produce a novel meaning. Specifically, they document the relationships between different syntactic and semantic categories, providing a bridge between the individual words and the compositional units. Baroni and Zamparelli (2010) proposed a supervised learning method that generalised the lexical function approach, allowing for the construction of novel compositional units through the application of well-defined statistical measures. This method provided a significant contribution to the field of distributional semantics, as it provided a systematic and empirically grounded method for composition. In this paper, we propose a novel method for composition, one that generalises the lexico-functional approach by Baroni and Zamparelli (2010). Our method builds on their ideas, incorporating several key insights that aim to improve the performance and scalability of composition. In particular, we draw on recent advances in representation learning, transfer learning, and large-scale evaluation frameworks. Our novel method is evaluated on a large-scale dataset that we developed specifically for the purpose of compositional tasks, allowing us to quantify the improvements brought about by our proposed method.

Recognizing Implicit Discourse Relations via Repeated Reading: Neural Networks with Multi-Level Attention Natural Language Processing (NLP) has witnessed tremendous growth in recent years, and one of its key areas is discourse relation recognition. Discourse relations help us understand how various parts of a passage interconnect and contribute to the overall meaning of the text. While explicit discourse relations can be gleaned from surface-level information, implicit discourse relations often require deeper semantic analysis to uncover. These relations are particularly challenging to identify, as they demand an understanding of not only the explicit content but also the underlying nuances of language. Recognizing implicit discourse relations is essential for numerous NLP applications, including document summarization, question-answering systems, and text analysis. Implicit discourse relations can take many forms, including similarities and contrasts, causality, conditionality, and others. For instance, consider the following example: "The increase in CO2 levels will lead to rising global temperatures. This will in turn accelerate the melting of polar ice caps, which has severe consequences for planetary ecosystems." In this passage, the clause "This will in turn accelerate..." introduces an implicit discourse relation indicating a causal link between the increase in CO2 levels and the rise in temperatures. To determine this relationship, one needs to carefully analyze the semantics and syntax of the text, setting it apart from surface-level information. Current state-of-the-art approaches to discourse relation recognition rely heavily on hand-crafted features such as Part-of-Speech (POS) tags, dependency parse trees, and word embeddings. However, although successful in capturing explicit features, they often fail to capture the complex, implicit relationships that lie beneath. In contrast to existing methods, our proposed approach recognizes the importance of modeling the repeated reading process, a cognitive strategy employed by human readers to comprehend complex texts. By applying this strategy, we believe that we can dynamically exploit critical features useful for identifying the underlying discourse relations. Inspired by recent advances in attention-based neural networks, we propose the Neural Networks with Multi-Level Attention (NNMA), which aims to mimic the repeated reading strategy through a multi-layered attention mechanism. Our model leverages external memories to aid in the integration of information across multiple levels of abstraction, effectively enabling the network to progressively focus on essential words and their relationships. This innovative approach encourages the network to reason both locally and globally, effectively traversing the nuanced semantic landscape of the input text.

Introduction The widespread use of social media platforms has led to a tremendous rise in user generated content, notably text. This informal nature of social media text though convenient for the masses, poses substantial challenges for natural language processing (NLP) tools. A significant problem arises when these tools fail to process and understand the informal language used on social media due to its ungrammatical and unconventional spellings, punctuation, and vocabulary. Standardizing this non-standard text into its canonical forms would significantly enhance the usability and interpretability of the content by various NLP tools and systems. Text normalization is a crucial task that aims to restore the non-standard words in a social media text document to their corresponding standard or canonical forms. Bydoing so, it significantly enhances the performance and accuracy of various downstream NLP applications such as sentiment analysis, named entity recognition, text classification, and information retrieval. Furthermore, normalization is typically the first step in any text processing pipeline, and it sets the tone for all subsequent tasks and analyses. Consequently, the quest for an effective text normalization technique has been an area of significant research interest in the NLP community. Traditional text normalization methods rely on a dictionary-based approach, which involves generating a pre-built list of non-standard words and their corresponding canonical forms. However, these methods have several drawbacks. Firstly, they require extensive manual effort and resources to build and maintain the normalization dictionaries. Secondly, they lack contextual sensitivity, failing to consider the actual usage and meanings of words in the input text. Thirdly, they may lead to over-correction or over-normalization, which can sometimes result in loss of nuances and original meanings. Recent advances in deep learning and graph-based methods have brought a new wave of interest to supervised and unsupervised text normalization approaches. These methods demonstrate the ability to learn complex patterns and relationships between words, both syntactically and semantically. Notably, they have the potential to handle out-of-vocabulary words and novel expressions that were traditionally difficult to address. Nevertheless, most of these recent approaches have several limitations. Firstly, they require substantial amounts of labeled training data, which can be challenging to obtain, especially for low-resource domains. Secondly, they often suffer from over-reliance on superficial word features, overlooking the grammatical and contextual nuances that are crucial for accurate normalization. In view of these challenges and limitations, this paper proposes an innovative unsupervised text normalization approach that tackles normalization as a graph-based problem.

Introduction Bilingual dictionary induction is a fundamental task in the field of natural language processing that aims to learn mapping functions between vector spaces of different languages. This task has the potential to break down language barriers and provide insights into the semantics of words across multiple languages. As a zero-shot learning task, bilingual dictionary induction allows us to learn mappings between languages where no bilingual dictionary or training data is available, which is especially important for low-resource languages. Given the significance of bilingual dictionary induction, several methods have been proposed to solve this task. However, most of these methods have focused on learning bilingual mappings directly from available bilingual data, which might not always be readily available for low-resource languages. Recently, the concept of using zero-shot learning to learn bilingual mappings between different languages has gained significant traction. The key idea is to leverage a shared space between languages, with word embeddings being the go-to approach to represent words in a dense, vectorial space. However, even methods that rely on zero-shot learning have not yet achieved high accuracy on the bilingual dictionary induction task. For example, in cases where the source and target languages exhibit syntactic, semantic, or morphological differences, current methods fail to learn robust bilingual mappings. This gap in current methods motivated our research into an alternative approach, which we term "bridging," to help cross the language barrier in bilingual dictionary induction. We identify two critical challenges in this endeavor. Firstly, we need to leverage rich translation resources to learn reliable bilingual mappings for low-resource languages. Secondly, we need an efficient and scalable way to add translation resources for new language pairs without disrupting the entire learning process. To address these challenges, we propose a novel knowledge distillation training objective, where rich resource translation paths are exploited as teachers, and low-resource language translation paths learn from these teachers. This approach not only introduces seamless addition of teacher translation paths for any given low-resource pair but also eliminates the tedious process of learning new bilingual mappings from scratch. However, we understand that the quality of the monolingual word embeddings will significantly affect the performance of bilingual dictionary induction. As such, we propose to enhance these vector representations with linguistic information to better capture the relationships between words in each language. By leveraging well-established linguistic resources, we can increase the dimensionality and quality of our vector embeddings, resulting in more accurate bilingual mappings.

Introduction The ability of a machine to engage in natural-sounding conversations with humans has captured the imagination of researchers and the public alike, and has sparked a flurry of activity in the field of natural language processing (NLP). Recent advances in deep learning have led to significant improvements in sequence-to-sequence (Seq2Seq) based dialogue systems, where a machine is trained to generate responses given a prompt or context. However, despite these advances, most current dialogue systems still struggle to produce responses that are coherent, engaging, and indistinguishable from human-generated dialogue. To push the boundaries of what is possible in dialogue generation, we draw inspiration from the classic Turing test (Turing, 1950). In this seminal work, Alan Turing proposed a test to determine whether a machine could exhibit intelligent behavior equivalent to, or indistinguishable from, that of a human. The Turing test consists of a human evaluator engaging in natural language conversations with both a human and a machine, without knowing which is which. If the evaluator cannot reliably distinguish the machine from the human, the test is passed. This gedankenexperiment has had a profound influence on the field of artificial intelligence (AI) and has remained relevant to this day, as researchers continue to strive for the holy grail of developing a machine that can truly converse like a human. In this paper, we propose a new approach to dialogue generation, drawing inspiration from the Turing test. We introduce a framework that leverages adversarial training to generate high-quality, human-like responses. Our approach is rooted in the understanding that a dialogue system should aim to produce sequences that are indistinguishable from human-generated dialogue utterances. To achieve this, we cast dialogue generation as a reinforcement learning (RL) problem, where a generative model is trained to produce response sequences, and a discriminator is used to distinguish between human-generated dialogues and machine-generated ones. The outputs from the discriminator serve as rewards for the generative model, guiding it to generate dialogues that resemble human dialogues. By leveraging the power of adversarial training, we create a more robust and sophisticated dialogue generation framework. The use of adversarial training in dialogue generation is particularly appealing, as it mirrors the process of human conversation, where interlocutors engage in a dynamic exchange of responses, each seeking to elicit a more informative and engaging response from the other. By jointly training the generative model and the discriminator, we enable the system to adapt and learn from the evaluations provided by the discriminator, much like a human would learn through conversations with others.

The quest for deep language understanding has been a persistent thread throughout the history of natural language processing (NLP). A fundamental challenge in this pursuit is the representation and learning of commonsense knowledge, which is essential for understanding casual and correlational relationships between events. While considerable progress has been made in advancing shallow language understanding, particularly in the areas of language modeling, sentiment analysis, and machine translation, the task of encoding and leveraging human-like commonsense knowledge remains an open problem. This difficulty is underscored by the countless instances of language models faltering or perplexing users with unexpected, yet statistically acceptable, responses to seemingly innocuous questions or prompts. A major hurdle in the field is the availability of an effective evaluation framework for studying story understanding and script learning, which are critical components of deep language understanding. Most existing evaluation benchmarks primarily focus on tasks such as question answering, text summarization, or sentiment analysis, where the goal is either to retrieve specific pieces of information or to flag superficial emotional nuances. These tasks, although undeniably important, skew the development of NLP systems in ways that compromise their ability to reason more deeply, cop to nuances of real world-scenarios, and effectively generalize across a relevant and diverse set of contexts. For story understanding and script learning in particular, the available evaluation frameworks are severely limited. The most common evaluation metrics rely on sentences as the unit of analysis, neglecting the intrinsic hierarchies of narrative structure that comprise stories. In addition, as our current understanding of commonsense knowledge and event interdependence quickly evolves, our evaluation procedures may not possess the flexibility and precision needed to assess the expanded capacity for real-world reasoning in our models. To create a more stringent and practically-oriented assessment framework, researchers have called for the development of more nuanced, and experiential-style tests that are capable of getting at whether or not a model has truly absorbed and understood a particular narrative context. In the paragraphs to follow, we propose a novel approach that starts to meet these criteria. By developing and testing our Story Cloze Test to evaluate story understanding and script learning, we are proposing that assessing causal/temporal relationships necessitates actual full positional internalization of a narrative structure, which has its native sense remembering ability free from grounded-state sensory perceptions.
